# const_format - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/const_format/

## Expand description

Compile-time string formatting.

This crate provides types and macros for formatting strings at compile-time.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-versions)Rust versions

There are some features that require a variety of Rust versions, the sections below describe the features that are available for each version.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-1710)Rust 1.71.0

These macros are available in Rust 1.71.0:

-
`concatcp``integers`,`bool`,`char`, and`&str`constants into a`&'static str`constant.
-
`formatcp``format``integers`,`bool`,`char`, and`&str`constants, and emits a`&'static str`constant.
-
`str_get``&'static str`constant, returning`None`when the index is out of bounds.
-
`str_index``&'static str`constant.
-
`str_repeat``&'static str`by repeating a`&'static str`constant`times`times.
-
`str_splice``&'static str`constant.
-
`map_ascii_case``&'static str`constant to a different casing style, determined by a`Case`
-
`str_replace``&'static str`constant with another`&'static str`constant.
-
`str_split`

The `"assertcp"` feature enables the [ assertcp](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_eq.html)

`assertcp_eq`[macros. These macros are like the standard library assert macros, but evaluated at compile-time, with the limitation that they can only have primitive types as arguments (just like](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html)

`assertcp_ne`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.concatcp.html)

`concatcp`[).](https://docs.rs/macro.formatcp.html)

`formatcp`[§](https://docs.rs#rust-1830)Rust 1.83.0

By enabling the “fmt” feature, you can use a [ std::fmt](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/index.html)-like API.

This requires Rust 1.83.0, because it uses mutable references in const fn.

All the other features of this crate are implemented on top of the [ const_format::fmt](https://docs.rs/fmt/index.html) API:

-
`concatc``&'static str`constant.
-
`formatc``format``&'static str`constant.
-
`writec``write``WriteMarker`

The `"derive"` feature enables the [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) macro,
and the

`"fmt"` feature.[derives the](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html)

`ConstDebug`[trait, and implements an inherent](https://docs.rs/marker_traits/trait.FormatMarker.html)

`FormatMarker``const_debug_fmt` method for compile-time debug formatting.The `"assertc"` feature enables the [ assertc](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc_eq.html)

`assertc_eq`[macros, and the](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc_ne.html)

`assertc_ne``"fmt"` feature.These macros are like the standard library assert macros, but evaluated at compile-time.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#concatenation-of-primitive-types)Concatenation of primitive types

```
use const_format::concatcp;
const NAME: &str = "Bob";
const FOO: &str = concatcp!(NAME, ", age ", 21u8,"!");
assert_eq!(FOO, "Bob, age 21!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-primitive-types)Formatting primitive types

```
use const_format::formatcp;
const NAME: &str = "John";
const FOO: &str = formatcp!("{NAME}, age {}!", compute_age(NAME));
assert_eq!(FOO, "John, age 24!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-custom-types)Formatting custom types

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro,
and then format the type into a

`&'static str` constant.This example requires the `"derive"` feature
and Rust 1.83.0, because it uses `&mut` in a const context.

```
use const_format::{ConstDebug, formatc};
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Message{
    ip: [Octet; 4],
    value: &'static str,
}
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Octet(u8);
const MSG: Message = Message{
    ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)],
    value: "Hello, World!",
};
const FOO: &str = formatc!("{:?}", MSG);
assert_eq!(
    FOO,
    "Message { ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)], value: \"Hello, World!\" }"
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatted-const-assertions)Formatted const assertions

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ assertcp_ne](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html) macro to
do compile-time inequality assertions with formatted error messages.

This requires the `"assertcp"` feature.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use const_format::assertcp_ne;
macro_rules! check_valid_pizza{
    ($user:expr, $topping:expr) => {
        assertcp_ne!(
            $topping,
            "pineapple",
            "You can't put pineapple on pizza, {}",
            $user,
        );
    }
}
check_valid_pizza!("John", "salami");
check_valid_pizza!("Dave", "sausage");
check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
```
This is the compiler output:

```
error[E0080]: evaluation of constant value failed
  --> src/lib.rs:178:27
   |
20 | check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
   |                           ^^^^^^^^^^^ the evaluated program panicked at '
assertion failed: `(left != right)`
 left: `"pineapple"`
right: `"pineapple"`
You can't put pineapple on pizza, Bob
', src/lib.rs:20:27
```
[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

All of the macros from `const_format` have these limitations:

-
The formatting macros that expand to `&'static str`s can only use constants from concrete types, so while a`Type::<u8>::FOO`argument would be fine,`Type::<T>::FOO`would not be (`T`being a type parameter).
-
Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context, [more details in the Integer arguments section](https://docs.rs#integer-args).
-
They cannot be used places that take string literals. So `#[doc = "foobar"]`cannot be replaced with`#[doc = concatcp!("foo", "bar") ]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#integer-arguments)Integer arguments

Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context. so if you only pass an integer literal it must have a suffix.

Example of what does compile:

```
const N: u32 = 1;
assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(N + 1, 2 + N), "23");
assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(2u32, 2 + 1u8, 3u8 + 1), "234");
```
Example of what does not compile:

[§](https://docs.rs#renaming-crate)Renaming crate

All function-like macros from `const_format` can be used when the crate is renamed.

The [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro has the

`#[cdeb(crate = "foo::bar")]` attribute to
tell it where to find the `const_format` crate.Example of renaming the `const_format` crate in the Cargo.toml file:

```
[dependencies]
cfmt = {version = "0.*", package = "const_format"}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo features

-
`"fmt"`: Enables the`std::fmt``"rust_1_83"`feature, requires Rust 1.83.0 because it uses mutable references in const fn.
 This feature includes the`formatc``writec`
-
`"derive"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, provides the`ConstDebug`
 This implicitly uses the`syn`crate, so clean compiles take a bit longer than without the feature.
-
`"assertc"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, enables the`assertc``assertc_eq``assertc_ne`
 This feature was previously named`"assert"`, but it was renamed to avoid confusion with the`"assertcp"`feature.
-
`"assertcp"`: Enables the`assertcp``assertcp_eq``assertcp_ne`
-
`"rust_1_83"`: Makes macros that evaluate to a value become compatible with[inline const patterns](https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.83.0/unstable-book/language-features/inline-const-pat.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

`const_format` is unconditionally `#![no_std]`, it can be used anywhere Rust can be used.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

`const_format` requires Rust 1.71.0.

Features that require newer versions of Rust, or the nightly compiler, need to be explicitly enabled with cargo features.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [ascii_](https://docs.rs/macro.ascii_str.html)- str - `fmt`
- Constructs an `AsciiStr`
- [assertc](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc.html)- `assertc`
- Compile-time assertions with formatting.
- [assertc_](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc_eq.html)- eq - `assertc`
- Compile-time equality assertion with formatting.
- [assertc_](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc_ne.html)- ne - `assertc`
- Compile-time inequality assertion with formatting.
- [assertcp](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp.html)- `assertcp`
- Compile-time assertion with formatting.
- [assertcp_](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_eq.html)- eq - `assertcp`
- Compile-time equality assertion with formatting.
- [assertcp_](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html)- ne - `assertcp`
- Compile-time inequality assertion with formatting.
- [call_](https://docs.rs/macro.call_debug_fmt.html)- debug_ - fmt - `fmt`
- For debug formatting of some specific generic std types, and other types.
- [coerce_](https://docs.rs/macro.coerce_to_fmt.html)- to_ - fmt - `fmt`
- Coerces a reference to a type that has a `const_*_fmt`method.
- [concatc](https://docs.rs/macro.concatc.html)- `fmt`
- Concatenates constants of standard library and/or user-defined types into a `&'static str`.
- [concatcp](https://docs.rs/macro.concatcp.html)
- Concatenates constants of primitive types into a `&'static str`.
- [formatc](https://docs.rs/macro.formatc.html)- `fmt`
- Formats constants of standard library and/or user-defined types into a `&'static str`.
- [formatcp](https://docs.rs/macro.formatcp.html)
- Formats constants of primitive types into a `&'static str`
- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_fmt.html)- fmt - `fmt`
- For implementing debug or display formatting “manually”.
- [map_](https://docs.rs/macro.map_ascii_case.html)- ascii_ - case
- Converts the casing style of a `&'static str`constant, ignoring non-ascii unicode characters.
- [str_get](https://docs.rs/macro.str_get.html)
- Indexes a `&'static str`constant, returning`None`when the index is not on a character boundary.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_index.html)- index
- Indexes a `&'static str`constant.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_repeat.html)- repeat
- Creates a `&'static str`by repeating a`&'static str`constant`times`times
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_replace.html)- replace
- Replaces all the instances of `$pattern`in`$input`(a`&'static str`constant) with`$replace_with`(a`&'static str`constant).
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_splice.html)- splice
- Replaces a substring in a `&'static str`constant. Returns both the new resulting`&'static str`, and the replaced substring.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_splice_out.html)- splice_ - out
- Alternative version of `str_splice`
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_split.html)- split
- Splits `$string`(a`&'static str`constant) with`$splitter`, returning an array of`&'static str`s.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_split_pat.html)- split_ - pat
- Version of `str_split``&'static [&'static str]`.
- [strwriter_](https://docs.rs/macro.strwriter_as_str.html)- as_ - str - Deprecated - `fmt`
- Converts a `&'static StrWriter`to a`&'static str`, in a`const`/`static`initializer.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_.html)- `fmt`
- For returning early on an error, otherwise evaluating to `()`.
- [unwrap](https://docs.rs/macro.unwrap.html)- `fmt`
- Equivalent to `Result::unwrap`, for use with`const_format::Error`
- [unwrap_](https://docs.rs/macro.unwrap_or_else.html)- or_ - else - `fmt`
- Equivalent to `Result::unwrap_or_else`but allows returning from the enclosing function.
- [writec](https://docs.rs/macro.writec.html)- `fmt`
- Writes some formatted standard library and/or user-defined types into a buffer.

- [coerce_](https://docs.rs/macro.coerce_to_fmt.html)- to_ - fmt - `fmt`
- Coerces a reference to a type that has a `const_*_fmt`method.
- [concatc](https://docs.rs/macro.concatc.html)- `fmt`
- Concatenates constants of standard library and/or user-defined types into a `&'static str`.
- [concatcp](https://docs.rs/macro.concatcp.html)
- Concatenates constants of primitive types into a `&'static str`.
- [formatc](https://docs.rs/macro.formatc.html)- `fmt`
- Formats constants of standard library and/or user-defined types into a `&'static str`.
- [formatcp](https://docs.rs/macro.formatcp.html)
- Formats constants of primitive types into a `&'static str`
- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_fmt.html)- fmt - `fmt`
- For implementing debug or display formatting “manually”.
- [map_](https://docs.rs/macro.map_ascii_case.html)- ascii_ - case
- Converts the casing style of a `&'static str`constant, ignoring non-ascii unicode characters.
- [str_get](https://docs.rs/macro.str_get.html)
- Indexes a `&'static str`constant, returning`None`when the index is not on a character boundary.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_index.html)- index
- Indexes a `&'static str`constant.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_repeat.html)- repeat
- Creates a `&'static str`by repeating a`&'static str`constant`times`times
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_replace.html)- replace
- Replaces all the instances of `$pattern`in`$input`(a`&'static str`constant) with`$replace_with`(a`&'static str`constant).
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_splice.html)- splice
- Replaces a substring in a `&'static str`constant. Returns both the new resulting`&'static str`, and the replaced substring.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_splice_out.html)- splice_ - out
- Alternative version of `str_splice`
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_split.html)- split
- Splits `$string`(a`&'static str`constant) with`$splitter`, returning an array of`&'static str`s.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_split_pat.html)- split_ - pat
- Version of `str_split``&'static [&'static str]`.
- [strwriter_](https://docs.rs/macro.strwriter_as_str.html)- as_ - str - Deprecated - `fmt`
- Converts a `&'static StrWriter`to a`&'static str`, in a`const`/`static`initializer.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_.html)- `fmt`
- For returning early on an error, otherwise evaluating to `()`.
- [unwrap](https://docs.rs/macro.unwrap.html)- `fmt`
- Equivalent to `Result::unwrap`, for use with`const_format::Error`
- [unwrap_](https://docs.rs/macro.unwrap_or_else.html)- or_ - else - `fmt`
- Equivalent to `Result::unwrap_or_else`but allows returning from the enclosing function.
- [writec](https://docs.rs/macro.writec.html)- `fmt`
- Writes some formatted standard library and/or user-defined types into a buffer.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

assertion failed: `(left != right)`

right: `"pineapple"`
You can't put pineapple on pizza, Bob
', src/lib.rs:20:27
```
# Limitations

All of the macros from `const_format` have these limitations:

-
The formatting macros that expand to `&'static str`s can only use constants from concrete types, so while a`Type::<u8>::FOO`argument would be fine,`Type::<T>::FOO`would not be (`T`being a type parameter).
-
Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context, [more details in the Integer arguments section](https://docs.rs#integer-args).
-
They cannot be used places that take string literals. So `#[doc = "foobar"]`cannot be replaced with`#[doc = concatcp!("foo", "bar") ]`.

### Integer arguments

Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context. so if you only pass an integer literal it must have a suffix.

Example of what does compile:

```
const N: u32 = 1;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
Example of what does not compile:

```
assert_eq!;
```

# Renaming crate

All function-like macros from `const_format` can be used when the crate is renamed.

The [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/const_format/0.2.*/const_format/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro has the

`#[cdeb(crate = "foo::bar")]` attribute to
tell it where to find the `const_format` crate.Example of renaming the `const_format` crate in the Cargo.toml file:

```
[]
 = { = "0.*",  = "const_format"}
```
# Cargo features

-
`"fmt"`: Enables the`std::fmt``"rust_1_83"`feature, requires Rust 1.83.0 because it uses mutable references in const fn. This feature includes the`formatc``writec`
-
`"derive"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, provides the`ConstDebug``syn`crate, so clean compiles take a bit longer than without the feature.
-
`"assertc"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, enables the`assertc``assertc_eq``assertc_ne``"assert"`, but it was renamed to avoid confusion with the`"assertcp"`feature.
-
`"assertcp"`: Enables the`assertcp``assertcp_eq``assertcp_ne`
-
`"rust_1_83"`: Makes macros that evaluate to a value become compatible with[inline const patterns](https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.83.0/unstable-book/language-features/inline-const-pat.html).

# No-std support

`const_format` is unconditionally `#![no_std]`, it can be used anywhere Rust can be used.

# Minimum Supported Rust Version

`const_format` requires Rust 1.71.0.

Features that require newer versions of Rust, or the nightly compiler, need to be explicitly enabled with cargo features.

# fastrand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fastrand/^1.3.5/

## Expand description

A simple and fast random number generator.

The implementation uses [Wyrand](https://github.com/wangyi-fudan/wyhash), a simple and fast
generator but **not** cryptographically secure.

Flip a coin:

```
if fastrand::bool() {
    println!("heads");
} else {
    println!("tails");
}
```
Generate a random `i32`:

`let num = fastrand::i32(..);`Choose a random element in an array:

```
let v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let i = fastrand::usize(..v.len());
let elem = v[i];
```
Shuffle an array:

```
let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
fastrand::shuffle(&mut v);
```
Generate a random [ Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html) or

[:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

`String````
use std::iter::repeat_with;
let v: Vec<i32> = repeat_with(|| fastrand::i32(..)).take(10).collect();
let s: String = repeat_with(fastrand::alphanumeric).take(10).collect();
```
To get reproducible results on every run, initialize the generator with a seed:

```
// Pick an arbitrary number as seed.
fastrand::seed(7);
// Now this prints the same number on every run:
println!("{}", fastrand::u32(..));
```
To be more efficient, create a new [ Rng](https://docs.rs/struct.Rng.html) instance instead of using the thread-local
generator:

```
use std::iter::repeat_with;
let rng = fastrand::Rng::new();
let mut bytes: Vec<u8> = repeat_with(|| rng.u8(..)).take(10_000).collect();
```

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#concatenation-of-primitive-types)Concatenation of primitive types

```
use const_format::concatcp;

[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-custom-types)Formatting custom types

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro,
and then format the type into a

`&'static str` constant.This example requires the `"derive"` feature
and Rust 1.83.0, because it uses `&mut` in a const context.

```
use const_format::{ConstDebug, formatc};
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Message{
    ip: [Octet; 4],
    value: &'static str,
}
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Octet(u8);
const MSG: Message = Message{
    ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)],
    value: "Hello, World!",
};
const FOO: &str = formatc!("{:?}", MSG);
assert_eq!(
    FOO,
    "Message { ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)], value: \"Hello, World!\" }"
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatted-const-assertions)Formatted const assertions

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ assertcp_ne](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html) macro to
do compile-time inequality assertions with formatted error messages.

This requires the `"assertcp"` feature.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use const_format::assertcp_ne;
macro_rules! check_valid_pizza{
    ($user:expr, $topping:expr) => {
        assertcp_ne!(
            $topping,
            "pineapple",
            "You can't put pineapple on pizza, {}",
            $user,
        );
    }
}
check_valid_pizza!("John", "salami");
check_valid_pizza!("Dave", "sausage");
check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
```
This is the compiler output:

```
error[E0080]: evaluation of constant value failed
  --> src/lib.rs:178:27
   |
20 | check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");

assertion failed: `(left != right)`
 left: `"pineapple"`
right: `"pineapple"`
You can't put pineapple on pizza, Bob
', src/lib.rs:20:27
```

- [coerce_](https://docs.rs/macro.coerce_to_fmt.html)- to_ - fmt - `fmt`
- Coerces a reference to a type that has a `const_*_fmt`method.
- [concatc](https://docs.rs/macro.concatc.html)- `fmt`
- Concatenates constants of standard library and/or user-defined types into a `&'static str`.
- [concatcp](https://docs.rs/macro.concatcp.html)
- Concatenates constants of primitive types into a `&'static str`.
- [formatc](https://docs.rs/macro.formatc.html)- `fmt`
- Formats constants of standard library and/or user-defined types into a `&'static str`.
- [formatcp](https://docs.rs/macro.formatcp.html)
- Formats constants of primitive types into a `&'static str`
- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_fmt.html)- fmt - `fmt`
- For implementing debug or display formatting “manually”.
- [map_](https://docs.rs/macro.map_ascii_case.html)- ascii_ - case
- Converts the casing style of a `&'static str`constant, ignoring non-ascii unicode characters.
- [str_get](https://docs.rs/macro.str_get.html)
- Indexes a `&'static str`constant, returning`None`when the index is not on a character boundary.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_index.html)- index
- Indexes a `&'static str`constant.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_repeat.html)- repeat
- Creates a `&'static str`by repeating a`&'static str`constant`times`times
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_replace.html)- replace
- Replaces all the instances of `$pattern`in`$input`(a`&'static str`constant) with`$replace_with`(a`&'static str`constant).
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_splice.html)- splice
- Replaces a substring in a `&'static str`constant. Returns both the new resulting`&'static str`, and the replaced substring.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_splice_out.html)- splice_ - out
- Alternative version of `str_splice`
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_split.html)- split
- Splits `$string`(a`&'static str`constant) with`$splitter`, returning an array of`&'static str`s.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_split_pat.html)- split_ - pat
- Version of `str_split``&'static [&'static str]`.
- [strwriter_](https://docs.rs/macro.strwriter_as_str.html)- as_ - str - Deprecated - `fmt`
- Converts a `&'static StrWriter`to a`&'static str`, in a`const`/`static`initializer.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_.html)- `fmt`
- For returning early on an error, otherwise evaluating to `()`.
- [unwrap](https://docs.rs/macro.unwrap.html)- `fmt`
- Equivalent to `Result::unwrap`, for use with`const_format::Error`
- [unwrap_](https://docs.rs/macro.unwrap_or_else.html)- or_ - else - `fmt`
- Equivalent to `Result::unwrap_or_else`but allows returning from the enclosing function.
- [writec](https://docs.rs/macro.writec.html)- `fmt`
- Writes some formatted standard library and/or user-defined types into a buffer.

# const_format - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/const_format/latest/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/const_format/

## Expand description

Compile-time string formatting.

This crate provides types and macros for formatting strings at compile-time.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-versions)Rust versions

There are some features that require a variety of Rust versions, the sections below describe the features that are available for each version.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-1710)Rust 1.71.0

These macros are available in Rust 1.71.0:

-
`concatcp``integers`,`bool`,`char`, and`&str`constants into a`&'static str`constant.
-
`formatcp``format``integers`,`bool`,`char`, and`&str`constants, and emits a`&'static str`constant.
-
`str_get``&'static str`constant, returning`None`when the index is out of bounds.
-
`str_index``&'static str`constant.
-
`str_repeat``&'static str`by repeating a`&'static str`constant`times`times.
-
`str_splice``&'static str`constant.
-
`map_ascii_case``&'static str`constant to a different casing style, determined by a`Case`
-
`str_replace``&'static str`constant with another`&'static str`constant.
-
`str_split`

The `"assertcp"` feature enables the [ assertcp](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_eq.html)

`assertcp_eq`[macros. These macros are like the standard library assert macros, but evaluated at compile-time, with the limitation that they can only have primitive types as arguments (just like](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html)

`assertcp_ne`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.concatcp.html)

`concatcp`[).](https://docs.rs/macro.formatcp.html)

`formatcp`[§](https://docs.rs#rust-1830)Rust 1.83.0

By enabling the “fmt” feature, you can use a [ std::fmt](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/index.html)-like API.

This requires Rust 1.83.0, because it uses mutable references in const fn.

All the other features of this crate are implemented on top of the [ const_format::fmt](https://docs.rs/fmt/index.html) API:

-
`concatc``&'static str`constant.
-
`formatc``format``&'static str`constant.
-
`writec``write``WriteMarker`

The `"derive"` feature enables the [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) macro,
and the

`"fmt"` feature.[derives the](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html)

`ConstDebug`[trait, and implements an inherent](https://docs.rs/marker_traits/trait.FormatMarker.html)

`FormatMarker``const_debug_fmt` method for compile-time debug formatting.The `"assertc"` feature enables the [ assertc](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc_eq.html)

`assertc_eq`[macros, and the](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc_ne.html)

`assertc_ne``"fmt"` feature.These macros are like the standard library assert macros, but evaluated at compile-time.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#concatenation-of-primitive-types)Concatenation of primitive types

```
use const_format::concatcp;
const NAME: &str = "Bob";
const FOO: &str = concatcp!(NAME, ", age ", 21u8,"!");
assert_eq!(FOO, "Bob, age 21!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-primitive-types)Formatting primitive types

```
use const_format::formatcp;
const NAME: &str = "John";
const FOO: &str = formatcp!("{NAME}, age {}!", compute_age(NAME));
assert_eq!(FOO, "John, age 24!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-custom-types)Formatting custom types

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro,
and then format the type into a

`&'static str` constant.This example requires the `"derive"` feature
and Rust 1.83.0, because it uses `&mut` in a const context.

```
use const_format::{ConstDebug, formatc};
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Message{
    ip: [Octet; 4],
    value: &'static str,
}
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Octet(u8);
const MSG: Message = Message{
    ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)],
    value: "Hello, World!",
};
const FOO: &str = formatc!("{:?}", MSG);
assert_eq!(
    FOO,
    "Message { ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)], value: \"Hello, World!\" }"
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatted-const-assertions)Formatted const assertions

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ assertcp_ne](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html) macro to
do compile-time inequality assertions with formatted error messages.

This requires the `"assertcp"` feature.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use const_format::assertcp_ne;
macro_rules! check_valid_pizza{
    ($user:expr, $topping:expr) => {
        assertcp_ne!(
            $topping,
            "pineapple",
            "You can't put pineapple on pizza, {}",
            $user,
        );
    }
}
check_valid_pizza!("John", "salami");
check_valid_pizza!("Dave", "sausage");
check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
```
This is the compiler output:

```
error[E0080]: evaluation of constant value failed
  --> src/lib.rs:178:27
   |
20 | check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
   |                           ^^^^^^^^^^^ the evaluated program panicked at '
assertion failed: `(left != right)`
 left: `"pineapple"`
right: `"pineapple"`
You can't put pineapple on pizza, Bob
', src/lib.rs:20:27
```
[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

All of the macros from `const_format` have these limitations:

-
The formatting macros that expand to `&'static str`s can only use constants from concrete types, so while a`Type::<u8>::FOO`argument would be fine,`Type::<T>::FOO`would not be (`T`being a type parameter).
-
Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context, [more details in the Integer arguments section](https://docs.rs#integer-args).
-
They cannot be used places that take string literals. So `#[doc = "foobar"]`cannot be replaced with`#[doc = concatcp!("foo", "bar") ]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#integer-arguments)Integer arguments

Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context. so if you only pass an integer literal it must have a suffix.

Example of what does compile:

```
const N: u32 = 1;
assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(N + 1, 2 + N), "23");
assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(2u32, 2 + 1u8, 3u8 + 1), "234");
```
Example of what does not compile:

[§](https://docs.rs#renaming-crate)Renaming crate

All function-like macros from `const_format` can be used when the crate is renamed.

The [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro has the

`#[cdeb(crate = "foo::bar")]` attribute to
tell it where to find the `const_format` crate.Example of renaming the `const_format` crate in the Cargo.toml file:

```
[dependencies]
cfmt = {version = "0.*", package = "const_format"}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo features

-
`"fmt"`: Enables the`std::fmt``"rust_1_83"`feature, requires Rust 1.83.0 because it uses mutable references in const fn.
 This feature includes the`formatc``writec`
-
`"derive"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, provides the`ConstDebug`
 This implicitly uses the`syn`crate, so clean compiles take a bit longer than without the feature.
-
`"assertc"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, enables the`assertc``assertc_eq``assertc_ne`
 This feature was previously named`"assert"`, but it was renamed to avoid confusion with the`"assertcp"`feature.
-
`"assertcp"`: Enables the`assertcp``assertcp_eq``assertcp_ne`
-
`"rust_1_83"`: Makes macros that evaluate to a value become compatible with[inline const patterns](https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.83.0/unstable-book/language-features/inline-const-pat.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

`const_format` is unconditionally `#![no_std]`, it can be used anywhere Rust can be used.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

`const_format` requires Rust 1.71.0.

Features that require newer versions of Rust, or the nightly compiler, need to be explicitly enabled with cargo features.

The [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro has the

`#[cdeb(crate = "foo::bar")]` attribute to
tell it where to find the `const_format` crate.Example of renaming the `const_format` crate in the Cargo.toml file:

```
[dependencies]
cfmt = {version = "0.*", package = "const_format"}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo features

-
`"fmt"`: Enables the`std::fmt``"rust_1_83"`feature, requires Rust 1.83.0 because it uses mutable references in const fn.
 This feature includes the`formatc``writec`
-
`"derive"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, provides the`ConstDebug`
 This implicitly uses the`syn`crate, so clean compiles take a bit longer than without the feature.
-
`"assertc"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, enables the`assertc``assertc_eq``assertc_ne`
 This feature was previously named`"assert"`, but it was renamed to avoid confusion with the`"assertcp"`feature.
-
`"assertcp"`: Enables the`assertcp``assertcp_eq``assertcp_ne`
-
`"rust_1_83"`: Makes macros that evaluate to a value become compatible with[inline const patterns](https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.83.0/unstable-book/language-features/inline-const-pat.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

`const_format` is unconditionally `#![no_std]`, it can be used anywhere Rust can be used.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

`const_format` requires Rust 1.71.0.

Features that require newer versions of Rust, or the nightly compiler, need to be explicitly enabled with cargo features.

# const_format - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/const_format/latest/target-redirect/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/const_format/

## Expand description

Compile-time string formatting.

This crate provides types and macros for formatting strings at compile-time.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-versions)Rust versions

There are some features that require a variety of Rust versions, the sections below describe the features that are available for each version.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-1710)Rust 1.71.0

These macros are available in Rust 1.71.0:

-
`concatcp``integers`,`bool`,`char`, and`&str`constants into a`&'static str`constant.
-
`formatcp``format``integers`,`bool`,`char`, and`&str`constants, and emits a`&'static str`constant.
-
`str_get``&'static str`constant, returning`None`when the index is out of bounds.
-
`str_index``&'static str`constant.
-
`str_repeat``&'static str`by repeating a`&'static str`constant`times`times.
-
`str_splice``&'static str`constant.
-
`map_ascii_case``&'static str`constant to a different casing style, determined by a`Case`
-
`str_replace``&'static str`constant with another`&'static str`constant.
-
`str_split`

The `"assertcp"` feature enables the [ assertcp](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_eq.html)

`assertcp_eq`[macros. These macros are like the standard library assert macros, but evaluated at compile-time, with the limitation that they can only have primitive types as arguments (just like](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html)

`assertcp_ne`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.concatcp.html)

`concatcp`[).](https://docs.rs/macro.formatcp.html)

`formatcp`[§](https://docs.rs#rust-1830)Rust 1.83.0

By enabling the “fmt” feature, you can use a [ std::fmt](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/index.html)-like API.

This requires Rust 1.83.0, because it uses mutable references in const fn.

All the other features of this crate are implemented on top of the [ const_format::fmt](https://docs.rs/fmt/index.html) API:

-
`concatc``&'static str`constant.
-
`formatc``format``&'static str`constant.
-
`writec``write``WriteMarker`

The `"derive"` feature enables the [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) macro,
and the

`"fmt"` feature.[derives the](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html)

`ConstDebug`[trait, and implements an inherent](https://docs.rs/marker_traits/trait.FormatMarker.html)

`FormatMarker``const_debug_fmt` method for compile-time debug formatting.The `"assertc"` feature enables the [ assertc](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc_eq.html)

`assertc_eq`[macros, and the](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc_ne.html)

`assertc_ne``"fmt"` feature.These macros are like the standard library assert macros, but evaluated at compile-time.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#concatenation-of-primitive-types)Concatenation of primitive types

```
use const_format::concatcp;
const NAME: &str = "Bob";
const FOO: &str = concatcp!(NAME, ", age ", 21u8,"!");
assert_eq!(FOO, "Bob, age 21!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-primitive-types)Formatting primitive types

```
use const_format::formatcp;
const NAME: &str = "John";
const FOO: &str = formatcp!("{NAME}, age {}!", compute_age(NAME));
assert_eq!(FOO, "John, age 24!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-custom-types)Formatting custom types

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro,
and then format the type into a

`&'static str` constant.This example requires the `"derive"` feature
and Rust 1.83.0, because it uses `&mut` in a const context.

```
use const_format::{ConstDebug, formatc};
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Message{
    ip: [Octet; 4],
    value: &'static str,
}
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Octet(u8);
const MSG: Message = Message{
    ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)],
    value: "Hello, World!",
};
const FOO: &str = formatc!("{:?}", MSG);
assert_eq!(
    FOO,
    "Message { ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)], value: \"Hello, World!\" }"
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatted-const-assertions)Formatted const assertions

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ assertcp_ne](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html) macro to
do compile-time inequality assertions with formatted error messages.

This requires the `"assertcp"` feature.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use const_format::assertcp_ne;
macro_rules! check_valid_pizza{
    ($user:expr, $topping:expr) => {
        assertcp_ne!(
            $topping,
            "pineapple",
            "You can't put pineapple on pizza, {}",
            $user,
        );
    }
}
check_valid_pizza!("John", "salami");
check_valid_pizza!("Dave", "sausage");
check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
```
This is the compiler output:

```
error[E0080]: evaluation of constant value failed
  --> src/lib.rs:178:27
   |
20 | check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
   |                           ^^^^^^^^^^^ the evaluated program panicked at '
assertion failed: `(left != right)`
 left: `"pineapple"`
right: `"pineapple"`
You can't put pineapple on pizza, Bob
', src/lib.rs:20:27
```
[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

All of the macros from `const_format` have these limitations:

-
The formatting macros that expand to `&'static str`s can only use constants from concrete types, so while a`Type::<u8>::FOO`argument would be fine,`Type::<T>::FOO`would not be (`T`being a type parameter).
-
Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context, [more details in the Integer arguments section](https://docs.rs#integer-args).
-
They cannot be used places that take string literals. So `#[doc = "foobar"]`cannot be replaced with`#[doc = concatcp!("foo", "bar") ]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#integer-arguments)Integer arguments

Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context. so if you only pass an integer literal it must have a suffix.

Example of what does compile:

```
const N: u32 = 1;
assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(N + 1, 2 + N), "23");
assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(2u32, 2 + 1u8, 3u8 + 1), "234");
```
Example of what does not compile:

[§](https://docs.rs#renaming-crate)Renaming crate

All function-like macros from `const_format` can be used when the crate is renamed.

The [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro has the

`#[cdeb(crate = "foo::bar")]` attribute to
tell it where to find the `const_format` crate.Example of renaming the `const_format` crate in the Cargo.toml file:

```
[dependencies]
cfmt = {version = "0.*", package = "const_format"}
```

-

 This feature was previously named`"assert"`, but it was renamed to avoid confusion with the`"assertcp"`feature.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

`const_format` is unconditionally `#![no_std]`, it can be used anywhere Rust can be used.

`assertc_ne``"fmt"` feature.These macros are like the standard library assert macros, but evaluated at compile-time.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#concatenation-of-primitive-types)Concatenation of primitive types

```
use const_format::concatcp;
const NAME: &str = "Bob";
const FOO: &str = concatcp!(NAME, ", age ", 21u8,"!");
assert_eq!(FOO, "Bob, age 21!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-primitive-types)Formatting primitive types

```
use const_format::formatcp;
const NAME: &str = "John";
const FOO: &str = formatcp!("{NAME}, age {}!", compute_age(NAME));
assert_eq!(FOO, "John, age 24!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-custom-types)Formatting custom types

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro,
and then format the type into a

`&'static str` constant.This example requires the `"derive"` feature
and Rust 1.83.0, because it uses `&mut` in a const context.

```
use const_format::{ConstDebug, formatc};
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Message{
    ip: [Octet; 4],
    value: &'static str,
}
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Octet(u8);
const MSG: Message = Message{
    ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)],
    value: "Hello, World!",
};
const FOO: &str = formatc!("{:?}", MSG);
assert_eq!(
    FOO,
    "Message { ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)], value: \"Hello, World!\" }"
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatted-const-assertions)Formatted const assertions

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ assertcp_ne](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html) macro to
do compile-time inequality assertions with formatted error messages.

This requires the `"assertcp"` feature.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use const_format::assertcp_ne;
macro_rules! check_valid_pizza{
    ($user:expr, $topping:expr) => {
        assertcp_ne!(
            $topping,
            "pineapple",
            "You can't put pineapple on pizza, {}",
            $user,
        );
    }
}
check_valid_pizza!("John", "salami");
check_valid_pizza!("Dave", "sausage");
check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
```
This is the compiler output:

```
error[E0080]: evaluation of constant value failed
  --> src/lib.rs:178:27
   |
20 | check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
   |                           ^^^^^^^^^^^ the evaluated program panicked at '
assertion failed: `(left != right)`
 left: `"pineapple"`
right: `"pineapple"`
You can't put pineapple on pizza, Bob
', src/lib.rs:20:27
```
[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

All of the macros from `const_format` have these limitations:

-
The formatting macros that expand to `&'static str`s can only use constants from concrete types, so while a`Type::<u8>::FOO`argument would be fine,`Type::<T>::FOO`would not be (`T`being a type parameter).
-
Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context, [more details in the Integer arguments section](https://docs.rs#integer-args).
-
They cannot be used places that take string literals. So `#[doc = "foobar"]`cannot be replaced with`#[doc = concatcp!("foo", "bar") ]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#integer-arguments)Integer arguments

Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context. so if you only pass an integer literal it must have a suffix.

Example of what does compile:

```
const N: u32 = 1;
assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(N + 1, 2 + N), "23");
assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(2u32, 2 + 1u8, 3u8 + 1), "234");
```
Example of what does not compile:

[§](https://docs.rs#renaming-crate)Renaming crate

All function-like macros from `const_format` can be used when the crate is renamed.

The [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro has the

`#[cdeb(crate = "foo::bar")]` attribute to
tell it where to find the `const_format` crate.Example of renaming the `const_format` crate in the Cargo.toml file:

```
[dependencies]
cfmt = {version = "0.*", package = "const_format"}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo features

-
`"fmt"`: Enables the`std::fmt``"rust_1_83"`feature, requires Rust 1.83.0 because it uses mutable references in const fn.
 This feature includes the`formatc``writec`
-
`"derive"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, provides the`ConstDebug`
 This implicitly uses the`syn`crate, so clean compiles take a bit longer than without the feature.
-
`"assertc"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, enables the`assertc``assertc_eq``assertc_ne`
 This feature was previously named`"assert"`, but it was renamed to avoid confusion with the`"assertcp"`feature.
-
`"assertcp"`: Enables the`assertcp``assertcp_eq``assertcp_ne`
-
`"rust_1_83"`: Makes macros that evaluate to a value become compatible with[inline const patterns](https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.83.0/unstable-book/language-features/inline-const-pat.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

`const_format` is unconditionally `#![no_std]`, it can be used anywhere Rust can be used.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

`const_format` requires Rust 1.71.0.

Features that require newer versions of Rust, or the nightly compiler, need to be explicitly enabled with cargo features.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# 🐂 Oxen

Create a world where everyone can contribute to an Artificial General Intelligence, starting with the data.

# 🌾 What is Oxen?

Oxen at its core is a data version control library, written in Rust. Its goals are to be fast, reliable, and easy to use. It's designed to be used in a variety of ways, from a simple command line tool, to a remote server to sync to, to integrations into other ecosystems such as [python](https://github.com/Oxen-AI/oxen-release).

# 📚 Documentation

The documentation for the Oxen.ai tool chain can be found [here](https://docs.oxen.ai).

## Speed up the build process

### Linux

*Note: Rust 1.90+ on  x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu  already uses an optimized linker by default. For other variants of Linux, the instructions below may speed things up.*

On Linux, you can use the [mold](https://github.com/rui314/mold) linker to speed up builds.

Then create `.cargo/config.toml` in your Oxen repo root with the following
content:

```
[]
 = ["-C", "link-arg=-fuse-ld=/usr/local/bin/ld64.mold"]
```
### macOS with Apple Silicon

**For macOS with Apple Silicon**, you can use the [lld](https://lld.llvm.org/) linker.

```
```
Then create `.cargo/config.toml` in your Oxen repo root with the following:

```
[]
 = [ "-C", "link-arg=-fuse-ld=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/ld64.lld", ]
```

# cu_memmon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cu-memmon/1.0.0/cu_memmon/

## Expand description

Per-task heap-allocation monitor for Copper.

`CuMemMon` consumes the [ CuMonitor::observe_alloc](https://docs.rs/cu29-runtime/1.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cu29_runtime/monitoring/trait.CuMonitor.html#method.observe_alloc) hook the runtime emits
around every task and bridge lifecycle step and reports:

- per-step allocation deltas (running totals + per-call peak),
- per-task lifetime balance (`alloc - dealloc`since the task’s`start`),
- a throttled `[mem]`one-liner from`process_copperlist`,
- a final per-task **leak report**at runtime shutdown.

Optional realtime-strict mode (`realtime_strict: true` in the monitor’s
RON config) latches any non-zero allocation observed during `Preprocess`,
`Process`, or `Postprocess` and surfaces it from the *following*
`process_copperlist` call as a `CuError`. In practice that is the very same
iteration’s `process_copperlist` (it runs after all the step hooks), so the
violation aborts the run within the same tick it occurred in. The runtime
treats the returned error as a fatal monitor error and shuts down cleanly
— unrelated task errors are not escalated by this path. The first violating
step in a copperlist wins (later violations in the same window are
observed but don’t overwrite the latched cause).

When the runtime is **not** built with `cu29/memory_monitoring`, the macro
emits no allocation scopes, so `observe_alloc` is never called. `CuMemMon`
detects this in two complementary ways:

- At `start()`it probes the public counter API (`cu29::monitoring::global_allocated_bytes``None`the runtime side is off and we warn immediately.
- If the runtime side is on but no `observe_alloc`ever fires (the macro side was built without the feature — possible when features are wired piecemeal instead of through the`cu29`umbrella), the first scheduled summary tick emits a one-shot warning.

# makechain_crypto - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/makechain-crypto/0.1.1/makechain_crypto/

## Expand description

Makechain cryptographic primitives — message envelopes, identity claims, and custody.

This crate sits at the boundary between Commonware-native cryptography (used inside consensus, P2P, and storage) and the Ethereum-ecosystem primitives required by Makechain’s identity and settlement layer.

[§](https://docs.rs#boundary-policy)Boundary policy

[§](https://docs.rs#commonware-native-ed25519-key-material-on-the-consensus--p2p-layer)Commonware-native (Ed25519 key material on the consensus / P2P layer)

Validator keys, the consensus engine, P2P handshakes, and follower verification
use `commonware_cryptography::ed25519::PrivateKey` / `PublicKey` / `Signature`
and the `Signer` / `Verifier` traits. Those signatures are namespaced via
`union_unique(namespace, msg)` and live entirely above the wire boundary.

[§](https://docs.rs#raw-ed25519-user-message-envelopes--messagers)Raw Ed25519 (user message envelopes — `message.rs`)

User-submitted message envelopes (`proto::Message`) carry a 32-byte signer pubkey
and a 64-byte signature over the BLAKE3 hash of `MessageData`. The signature is
**raw RFC 8032 Ed25519** over the hash — no namespace, no wrapping. This wire
format is part of the protocol and is reflected in chain history.

`commonware_cryptography::ed25519::PrivateKey` cannot be used here because its
public `Signer::sign(namespace, msg)` always prepends a length-prefixed namespace
via `union_unique`. There is no public bypass — the raw `ed25519_consensus::SigningKey`
is held inside a `Secret<...>` field. Migrating envelope signing to the Commonware
`Signer` trait would change the wire bytes of every user message and invalidate
every signature already on chain.

As a result, [ message::build_message](https://docs.rs/message/fn.build_message.html) /

[keep](https://docs.rs/message/fn.verify_message.html)

`message::verify_message``ed25519-dalek` directly. The two wire formats coexist deliberately:
Commonware-namespaced for consensus / P2P, raw for the user envelope.[§](https://docs.rs#ethereum-ecosystem-verify_custodyrs-verify_claimrs)Ethereum ecosystem (`verify_custody.rs`, `verify_claim.rs`)

EIP-712 signing hashes, `secp256k1` ECDSA recovery, P256 / `WebAuthn` passkey
verification, and Keccak256 hashing are kept on raw `k256` / `p256` / `sha3`.
Commonware does not target the Ethereum stack, so there is no Commonware
equivalent for these paths.

The Solana Ed25519 sub-path inside [ verify_claim](https://docs.rs/verify_claim/index.html) is wire-compatible with raw
Ed25519 (the public key

*is*the Solana address) and could in principle migrate to

`commonware_cryptography::ed25519::PublicKey::verify`, but that runs into the
same namespace-wrapping issue: the Solana signature is over the raw challenge
bytes, not `union_unique(b"", challenge)`. It therefore stays on `ed25519-dalek`.[§](https://docs.rs#hexrs)`hex.rs`

Pure encode / decode helpers. No Commonware equivalent; nothing to migrate.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [account_](https://docs.rs/account_keychain/index.html)- keychain
- Makechain `AccountKeychain`custody primitives.
- [hex](https://docs.rs/hex/index.html)
- Hex encoding utilities used across the codebase.
- [message](https://docs.rs/message/index.html)
- [vcs_](https://docs.rs/vcs_sign/index.html)- sign
- [verify_](https://docs.rs/verify_claim/index.html)- claim
- Cryptographic verification of external identity claims.
- [verify_](https://docs.rs/verify_custody/index.html)- custody
- Ethereum/P256 address and signature helpers retained for local claim parsing.

# rutle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rutle/0.2.1/rutle/

## Expand description

`rutle` — Rob’s Universal Text Layout Engine: a rendering-agnostic structured
editor and layout core for [ tdoc::Document](https://docs.rs/tdoc/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tdoc/document/struct.Document.html).

The engine is organized as four layers, each depending only on the ones below it, so the same document logic drives any frontend:

- `Editor`- **editing engine**. Owns the authoritative- `tdoc::Document`
- **Layout**— the layout phase of- `Renderer`- `layout_*`): turns the document plus font metrics into positioned lines, runs, and table grids.
- **Paint**— the rendering phase of- `Renderer`- `draw_*`): walks the layout and emits drawing primitives.- `Renderer`
- `RenderContext`- **backend**trait a frontend implements to supply real text metrics (- `text_width`/- `text_height`/…) and drawing (- `draw_text`/- `draw_rect_filled`/…). The engine is agnostic to it: a GUI toolkit, a terminal cell grid, or the SVG backend used by the snapshot tests all plug in here.

This crate is the shared editing/layout core carved out of the
[Piki](https://github.com/roblillack/piki) editor.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_ALLOWED_PROJECTS.html)- ALLOWED_ - PROJECTS
- Maximum `allowed_projects`entries in a scoped`SIGNER_ADD`/ keychain authorization. Shared by codec (decode bound), crypto (digest input), and state validation — single source of truth (was duplicated across all three).
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_CLAIM_SIGNATURE_LEN.html)- CLAIM_ - SIGNATURE_ - LEN
- Maximum `VERIFICATION_ADD`claim signature length.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_FINALIZATION_CERT_LEN.html)- FINALIZATION_ - CERT_ - LEN
- Maximum `STORAGE_CLAIM`finalization-certificate length.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_HEADER_RLP_LEN.html)- HEADER_ - RLP_ - LEN
- Maximum `STORAGE_CLAIM`RLP block-header length.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_KEYCHAIN_PUBLIC_KEY_LEN.html)- KEYCHAIN_ - PUBLIC_ - KEY_ - LEN
- Maximum explicit custody public key material length (secp256k1 uncompressed SEC1 is the largest at 65 bytes; P256/WebAuthn carry 64).
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_KEYCHAIN_SIGNATURE_LEN.html)- KEYCHAIN_ - SIGNATURE_ - LEN
- Canonical `AccountKeychain`length limits, shared across the codec (decode ceilings), crypto (digest input bounds), and state validation (structural caps) so the three layers cannot drift. The TS encoder mirrors these values (`packages/makechain-sdk/src/proto/encode.ts`).
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_KEYCHAIN_WITNESS_LEN.html)- KEYCHAIN_ - WITNESS_ - LEN
- Maximum opaque keychain witness (TIP-1053-style challenge binding; inert in v1). Bounds the signed digest input and the stored/wire body.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_PARENT_COMMITS.html)- PARENT_ - COMMITS
- Maximum parent commits per commit in a `COMMIT_BUNDLE`. Enforced canonically at the codec`read`boundary (`codec.rs`,`values.rs`) AND at message validation (`makechain_state::validation`) so the ingress/buffa path matches the canonical-codec decode bound. Single source of truth (was duplicated as a private const in`makechain-proto`and`makechain-state`).
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_PROOF_NODES.html)- PROOF_ - NODES
- Maximum `STORAGE_CLAIM`receipts-trie inclusion-proof node count.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_PROOF_NODE_LEN.html)- PROOF_ - NODE_ - LEN
- Maximum `STORAGE_CLAIM`receipts-trie inclusion-proof node length.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_RECEIPT_RLP_LEN.html)- RECEIPT_ - RLP_ - LEN
- Maximum `STORAGE_CLAIM`RLP receipt length.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_SIGNER_VALIDITY_WINDOW_SECS.html)- SIGNER_ - VALIDITY_ - WINDOW_ - SECS
- Maximum accepted validity window for `SIGNER_ADD`/`SIGNER_REMOVE`custody signatures (1 hour). Used by validation and client crates.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_WEBAUTHN_ENVELOPE_LEN.html)- WEBAUTHN_ - ENVELOPE_ - LEN
- Maximum `WebAuthn`custody envelope length (`DoS`bound on the custody-verify path).
- [PROTOCOL_](https://docs.rs/constant.PROTOCOL_VERSION.html)- VERSION
- Canonical protocol version carried in block headers.
- [STORAGE_](https://docs.rs/constant.STORAGE_GRANT_TOTAL_SECS.html)- GRANT_ - TOTAL_ - SECS
- Duration in seconds for an active storage grant plus grace period (approximately 13 months).

# kigumi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kigumi/0.1.0/kigumi/

## Expand description

Facade for the Kigumi framework. Application modules depend only on this crate.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use kigumi_core::`- [inventory](https://docs.rs/inventory/0.3.24/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/inventory/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Everything needed to define a module: `use kigumi::prelude::*;`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_acls.html)- acls
- Registers a module’s ACLs so a server collects them via `registered_acls()`. Use at module top level:`kigumi::register_acls!(ACLS);`where`ACLS: &'static [Acl]`.
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_action.html)- action
- Registers a state-transition action on a model, runnable via `POST /api/<model>/<id>/action/<name>`.`kigumi::register_action!("sale.order", "confirm", confirm_order, &["sales.user"]);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_compute.html)- compute
- Registers a compute function by name, so the engine runs it on write for fields declaring it.
Use at module top level: `kigumi::register_compute!("compute_total", compute_total);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_constraint.html)- constraint
- Registers a cross-record constraint (Odoo `@api.constrains`):`func`runs in the write transaction after the record + its children are written, and returns`Err(msg)`to reject (roll back) the write.`fields`are the triggers (empty = every write); list the WRITTEN fields and One2many field names that drive the invariant, plus any stored computed field it reads (those also trigger on update). Use at module top level:`kigumi::register_constraint!("account.move", &["line_ids"], check_balanced);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_external.html)- external
- Marks a model’s table as owned outside the metamodel (Odoo’s `_auto = False`): the model is resolved/served normally but migration never creates or alters its table. For models mapped onto a pre-existing table (e.g.`res.users`onto the auth subsystem’s`kigumi_user`) or a SQL view. Use at module top level:`kigumi::register_external!("res.users");`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_field_groups.html)- field_ - groups
- Restricts a model field to the given groups (D6 field-level security): read AND write of that
field require membership in at least one group; superuser bypasses. Usually emitted automatically
by `#[field(groups = "...")]`, but can be declared by hand:`kigumi::register_field_groups!("res.users", "login", &["admin"]);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_inherits.html)- inherits
- Declares delegation inheritance (Odoo’s `_inherits`):`model`exposes`parent`’s stored scalar fields through its required Many2one`via`FK. Usually emitted by`#[model(inherits=…, via=…)]`:`kigumi::register_inherits!("product.product", "product.template", "product_tmpl_id");`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_job.html)- job
- Registers a BACKGROUND JOB kind, runnable ad hoc with retries: enqueue with
`Db::enqueue_job(name, payload)`or — transactionally, inside a service — with`ServiceCtx::enqueue_job`.`func`is an`async fn(&Db, Json) -> Result<(), DbError>`; a returned Err retries with exponential backoff up to`max_attempts`(then dead-letters). Bodies MUST be idempotent (at-least-once execution).`kigumi::register_job!("send_invoice_mail", 8, send_mail);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_ledger_report.html)- ledger_ - report
- Registers a read-only LEDGER REPORT (record-less aggregate query, returning JSON rows) runnable via
`GET /api/reports/<name>`— distinct from`register_report!`, which is the per-record document/PDF engine.`func`is an`async fn(&PgPool, params) -> Result<Vec<Json>, DbError>`;`read_model`is the model whose Read ACL gates it. The macro emits the one`Box::pin`adapting the async fn to the fn ptr.`kigumi::register_ledger_report!("trial_balance", "account.account", trial_balance, &[]);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_mailed.html)- mailed
- Opts a model into the mail subsystem (chatter): it gains a thread of messages, followers and
activities via the `(res_model, res_id)`link, and the framework cleans that thread up when the record is deleted. One line, no mixin:`kigumi::register_mailed!("sale.order");`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_migration.html)- migration
- Registers a versioned DATA migration for a module — the upgrade contract. It runs when migrate
finds the module installed at a ledger version < `to_version`while the linked crate is
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_module.html)- module
- Registers a module’s manifest in the global catalog, so `resolve_modules`can see it. Use at module top level:`kigumi::register_module!(MANIFEST);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_related.html)- related
- Marks a field as a `related`field (Odoo`related=`): a non-stored, read-only mirror of the value reached by`path`(e.g. “order_id.currency_id”). Usually emitted by`#[field(related = "...")]`.`kigumi::register_related!("sale.order.line", "order_currency_id", "order_id.currency_id");`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_report.html)- report
- Registers a report on a model: a pure render fn producing an HTML document for one record, exposed
at `GET /api/<model>/<id>/report/<name>`(secured by read access to the record) and listed in the model’s UI contract.`name`is the URL segment,`title`the human label. Use at module top level:`kigumi::register_report!("sale.order", "quotation", "Quotation", render_quotation);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_route.html)- route
- Registers a MODULE HTTP ROUTE on the generic dispatch `GET|POST /api/x/<name>`— bespoke module endpoints (an inbound-webhook receiver, a custom search) without the module ever depending on the server crate or axum.`method`is a RouteMethod variant name (Get|Post);`auth: false`runs the body under the GUEST context (uid −1, no groups — the default-deny ACL blocks every secured call, so verify the sender yourself — use`RouteInput::verify_hmac_sha256`or your provider’s exact scheme with a CONSTANT-TIME comparison, never a hand-rolled hash +`==`— then elevate via`.sudo()`. Query/body/header values are anonymous input: bind them in SQL, never interpolate).`kigumi::register_route!("stripe-hook", Post, false, &[], stripe_hook);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_rules.html)- rules
- Registers a module’s record rules so a server collects them via `registered_rules()`. Use at module top level:`kigumi::register_rules!(RULES);`where`RULES: &'static [RecordRule]`.
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_seed.html)- seed
- Registers a module’s idempotent reference-data seeder, run at every migrate while the module
is installed (in dependency order). Bodies must never overwrite operator changes — guard with
count/exists checks: the DB is the authority. `func`is an`async fn(&Db) -> Result<(), DbError>`.`kigumi::register_seed!("base", seed::seed_base_data);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_sequence.html)- sequence
- Registers a document-numbering sequence, declared by the module whose action consumes it
(`ActionOutcome::assign_sequence`). Ensured at migrate; an existing sequence keeps its counter.`kigumi::register_sequence!("sales", "SO", "SO/", "", 5);`→ SO/00001.
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_service.html)- service
- Registers a cross-record SERVICE on a model, runnable via `POST /api/<model>/<id>/service/<name>`. The transactional twin of`register_action!`:`func`is a`async fn(&mut ServiceCtx, ServiceInput) -> Result<ServiceOutput, DbError>`that owns multi-record logic through the secured`ServiceCtx`.`write_gate`is`true`for a mutating service,`false`for a read-only one (a report). The macro emits the one`Box::pin`that adapts the async fn to the stored fn pointer.`kigumi::register_service!("sale.order.discount", "apply_discount", apply_discount, true, &["sales.user"]);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_tracked.html)- tracked
- Marks a field as tracked (Odoo’s `tracking=True`): a change to it on a mailed model records a`notification`message + a typed`mail.tracking`row in the chatter. Usually emitted by`#[field(tracked)]`, but can be declared by hand:`kigumi::register_tracked!("sale.order", "state");`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_transient.html)- transient
- Marks a model as transient (Odoo’s `TransientModel`): a wizard scratchpad whose rows are ephemeral. The model is served + secured like any model, but an hourly GC cron reclaims rows by age, and migration gives its`create_date`column a`DEFAULT now()`so every insert is stamped. The model must declare a nullable`create_date: Datetime`. One line:`kigumi::register_transient!("sale.order.discount");`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_view.html)- view
- Registers a model’s form layout (Odoo’s form arch, minimal): titled groups of scalar fields plus a
notebook of tabbed pages. Emitted in the model’s UI contract so the frontend renders a real view
instead of dumping fields in declaration order. Use at module top level:
`kigumi::register_view!("product.product", &[ FieldGroup { .. } ], &[ NotebookPage { .. } ]);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_wizard.html)- wizard
- Registers a wizard: binds a transient `model`to its`default_get`(the server-side seed computed from the open context), exposing`POST /api/<model>/open`. The model must also be`register_transient!`-marked. Apply logic is a dedicated per-wizard service method + endpoint (like`apply_pricelist`), not part of this registration. Use at module top level:`kigumi::register_wizard!("sale.order.discount", default_get_discount);`
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_write_trigger.html)- write_ - trigger
- Registers an in-tx WRITE TRIGGER: `func`runs on the caller’s transaction after a secured write to`model`when one of`watch`columns changed (empty = every write), for a stored effect the`depends`recompute can’t express on read — e.g. a Many2many aggregate summed across a join.`func`is an`async fn(&mut Transaction, id, changed_cols) -> Result<(), DbError>`; a returned`Err`rolls the write back. The macro emits the one`Box::pin`adapting the async fn to the stored fn pointer.`kigumi::register_write_trigger!("product.template.attribute.value", &["price_extra"], recompute);`
