# dcb_layer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/dcb-layer/0.2.1/dcb_layer/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#dcb)dcb

A [DCB-compliant](https://dcb.events) event store backed by [FoundationDB](https://www.foundationdb.org).

Events are appended atomically, assigned a globally ordered [ Versionstamp](https://docs.rs/type.Versionstamp.html) position,
and indexed for fast retrieval by type, tags, or both.
Optimistic concurrency is enforced through

[s that fail the write if matching events appeared since the caller last read.](https://docs.rs/struct.AppendCondition.html)

`AppendCondition`[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

```
use dcb_layer::{Event, FdbStore, Query, QueryItem};
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // 1. Open a FoundationDB database (see foundationdb-rs for setup).
    let _network = unsafe { foundationdb::boot() };
    let db = foundationdb::Database::default().unwrap();
    // 2. Create a namespaced store — namespace isolates data within one FDB cluster.
    let store = FdbStore::new(db, "my-app");
    // 3. Append events (no condition = unconditional write).
    let event = Event::new(
        "OrderPlaced",
        ["order:42", "customer:7"],
        b"{\"total\":99}".as_slice(),
    );
    let position = store.append(vec![event], vec![]).await.unwrap();
    // 4. Read events back — filter by type, tags, or both.
    let results = store
        .read(
            Query {
                items: vec![QueryItem {
                    types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()],
                    tags: vec!["customer:7".into()],
                }],
            },
            None,
        )
        .await
        .unwrap();
    println!("Found {} event(s), first at {:?}", results.len(), results[0].position);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#core-concepts)Core concepts

[§](https://docs.rs#event)Event

An [ Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html) carries three fields, constructed via

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html#method.new)

`Event::new`| Field | Accepts | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `type_name` | `&str`/`String` | Required, non-empty (e.g. `"OrderPlaced"`) |
| `tags` | any iterable of strings | Up to 10 tags; `"_"`is reserved |
| `data` | `&[u8]`/`Vec<u8>` | Opaque bytes — encode however you like |

Tags are free-form strings. A common convention is `"entity:id"` (e.g. `"order:42"`),
but the store treats them as opaque labels.

[§](https://docs.rs#query)Query

A [ Query](https://docs.rs/struct.Query.html) is a list of

[s joined by](https://docs.rs/struct.QueryItem.html)

`QueryItem`**OR**. Each item matches events that satisfy

**all**of its constraints:

- `types`— event’s- `type_name`must be one of these (empty = any type)
- `tags`— event must carry- **all**of these tags (empty = any tags)

Every item must specify at least one type or one tag.

```
use dcb_layer::{Query, QueryItem};
// Match OrderPlaced OR OrderCancelled events tagged with order:42
let query = Query {
    items: vec![
        QueryItem { types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()], tags: vec!["order:42".into()] },
        QueryItem { types: vec!["OrderCancelled".into()], tags: vec!["order:42".into()] },
    ],
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#appendcondition)AppendCondition

An [ AppendCondition](https://docs.rs/struct.AppendCondition.html) guards a write with an optimistic-concurrency check:
the

`append` call fails with [if any event matching](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.AppendConditionFailed)

`Error::AppendConditionFailed``query` exists **after**the

`after` position (or at all, when `after` is `None`).The typical pattern:

- Read events matching your query → note the last position seen.
- Build your decision model from those events.
- Append new events with `after = last_position`to guard against concurrent writes.

```
use dcb_layer::{AppendCondition, Event, FdbStore, Query, QueryItem};
// 1. Read events and note the last position seen.
let results = store.read(
    Query { items: vec![QueryItem { types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()], tags: vec!["order:42".into()] }] },
    None,
).await.unwrap();
let last_position = results.last().map(|e| e.position);
// 2. Append new events — fail if a concurrent write snuck in after last_position.
let condition = AppendCondition {
    query: Query {
        items: vec![QueryItem {
            types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()],
            tags: vec!["order:42".into()],
        }],
    },
    after: last_position,
};
store.append(vec![Event::new("OrderPlaced", ["order:42"], b"".as_slice())], vec![condition]).await.unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#readoptions)ReadOptions

[ ReadOptions](https://docs.rs/struct.ReadOptions.html) controls pagination and ordering:

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `limit` | `0`(unlimited) | Maximum events to return |
| `after` | `None` | Only return events after this position |
| `reverse` | `false` | Newest-first when `true` |

[§](https://docs.rs#limits)Limits

| Constraint | Value |
|---|---|
| Max events per `append`call | 65 535 |
| Max tags per event | 10 |
| Reserved tag value | `"_"` |

[§](https://docs.rs#practical-sizing)Practical sizing

Each event writes one index key per **subset** of its tags (2^n keys for
n tags — up to 1 024 for 10 tags). All writes of an `append` call share one
FDB transaction, which is capped at 10 MB of affected data and 5 seconds —
keep batches small when events carry many tags.

Reads run in a single FDB transaction too: an unbounded [ FdbStore::read](https://docs.rs/struct.FdbStore.html#method.read)
or

[over a large store fails with](https://docs.rs/struct.FdbStore.html#method.read_all)

`FdbStore::read_all``transaction_too_old` (FDB error 1007) after a bounded number of retries.
Paginate with

`ReadOptions``limit` + `after`.Subscription cursors ([ FdbStore::set_cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.FdbStore.html#method.set_cursor)) are last-writer-wins; run
one consumer per cursor name or coordinate externally.

[§](https://docs.rs#foundationdb-setup)FoundationDB setup

This crate wraps the [ foundationdb](https://docs.rs/foundationdb) crate.
You are responsible for:

- installing and running an FDB cluster
- calling `unsafe { foundationdb::boot() }`once at startup (keeps the network thread alive)
- opening a `foundationdb::Database``FdbStore::new`

Refer to the [foundationdb-rs documentation](https://docs.rs/foundationdb) and
the [FoundationDB developer guide](https://apple.github.io/foundationdb/getting-started-linux.html)
for cluster setup and client configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#fdb-api-version)FDB API version

The default Cargo feature targets FDB 7.4. To use FDB 7.3, disable the default features:

`dcb-layer = { version = "...", default-features = false, features = ["fdb-7_3"] }`The feature selects the C API headers compiled against; a newer `libfdb_c` is backward compatible.

- [Versionstamp](https://docs.rs/type.Versionstamp.html)
- 12-byte globally unique, monotonically increasing position. Bytes 0–9: FDB transaction version (big-endian). Bytes 10–11: user version = batch index (big-endian u16).

# hdf5_metno - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hdf5-metno/0.13.0/hdf5_metno/

## Expand description

HDF5 for Rust.

This crate provides thread-safe Rust bindings and high-level wrappers for the `HDF5`
library API. Some of the features include:

- Thread-safety with non-threadsafe libhdf5 builds guaranteed via reentrant mutexes.
- Native representation of most HDF5 types, including variable-length strings and arrays.
- Derive-macro for automatic mapping of user structs and enums to `HDF5`types.
- Multi-dimensional array reading/writing interface via `ndarray`.

Direct low-level bindings are also available and provided in the `hdf5-sys` crate.

Requires `HDF5` library of version 1.8.4 or later. Newer versions will enable additional
features of the library. Such items are marked in the documentation with a version number
indicating the required version of `HDF5`. The `have-direct` and `have-parallel` features
also indicates `HDF5` functionality.

### Formatted const assertions

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ assertcp_ne](https://docs.rs/const_format/0.2.*/const_format/macro.assertcp_ne.html) macro to
do compile-time inequality assertions with formatted error messages.

use assertcp_ne;

This is the compiler output:

```
error[E0080]: evaluation of constant value failed
  --> src/lib.rs:178:27
   |
20 | check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
   |                           ^^^^^^^^^^^ the evaluated program panicked at '
assertion failed: `(left != right)`
 left: `"pineapple"`
right: `"pineapple"`
You can't put pineapple on pizza, Bob
', src/lib.rs:20:27
```
# Limitations

All of the macros from `const_format` have these limitations:

-
The formatting macros that expand to `&'static str`s can only use constants from concrete types, so while a`Type::<u8>::FOO`argument would be fine,`Type::<T>::FOO`would not be (`T`being a type parameter).
-
Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context, [more details in the Integer arguments section](https://docs.rs#integer-args).
-
They cannot be used places that take string literals. So `#[doc = "foobar"]`cannot be replaced with`#[doc = concatcp!("foo", "bar") ]`.

### Integer arguments

Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context. so if you only pass an integer literal it must have a suffix.

Example of what does compile:

```
const N: u32 = 1;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
Example of what does not compile:

```
assert_eq!;
```

None right now.

# Renaming crate

All function-like macros from `const_format` can be used when the crate is renamed.

The [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/const_format/0.2.*/const_format/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro has the

`#[cdeb(crate = "foo::bar")]` attribute to
tell it where to find the `const_format` crate.Example of renaming the `const_format` crate in the Cargo.toml file:

```
[]
 = { = "0.*",  = "const_format"}
```
# Cargo features

-
`"fmt"`: Enables the`std::fmt``"rust_1_83"`feature, requires Rust 1.83.0 because it uses mutable references in const fn. This feature includes the`formatc``writec`
-
`"derive"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, provides the`ConstDebug``syn`crate, so clean compiles take a bit longer than without the feature.
-
`"assertc"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, enables the`assertc``assertc_eq``assertc_ne``"assert"`, but it was renamed to avoid confusion with the`"assertcp"`feature.
-
`"assertcp"`: Enables the`assertcp``assertcp_eq``assertcp_ne`
-
`"rust_1_83"`: Makes macros that evaluate to a value become compatible with[inline const patterns](https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.83.0/unstable-book/language-features/inline-const-pat.html).

# No-std support

`const_format` is unconditionally `#![no_std]`, it can be used anywhere Rust can be used.

# Minimum Supported Rust Version

`const_format` requires Rust 1.71.0.

Features that require newer versions of Rust, or the nightly compiler, need to be explicitly enabled with cargo features.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#concatenation-of-primitive-types)Concatenation of primitive types

```
use const_format::concatcp;
const NAME: &str = "Bob";
const FOO: &str = concatcp!(NAME, ", age ", 21u8,"!");
assert_eq!(FOO, "Bob, age 21!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-primitive-types)Formatting primitive types

```
use const_format::formatcp;
const NAME: &str = "John";
const FOO: &str = formatcp!("{NAME}, age {}!", compute_age(NAME));
assert_eq!(FOO, "John, age 24!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-custom-types)Formatting custom types

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro,
and then format the type into a

`&'static str` constant.This example requires the `"derive"` feature
and Rust 1.83.0, because it uses `&mut` in a const context.

```
use const_format::{ConstDebug, formatc};
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Message{
    ip: [Octet; 4],
    value: &'static str,
}
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Octet(u8);
const MSG: Message = Message{
    ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)],
    value: "Hello, World!",
};
const FOO: &str = formatc!("{:?}", MSG);
assert_eq!(
    FOO,
    "Message { ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)], value: \"Hello, World!\" }"
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatted-const-assertions)Formatted const assertions

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ assertcp_ne](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html) macro to
do compile-time inequality assertions with formatted error messages.

This requires the `"assertcp"` feature.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use const_format::assertcp_ne;
macro_rules! check_valid_pizza{
    ($user:expr, $topping:expr) => {
        assertcp_ne!(
            $topping,
            "pineapple",
            "You can't put pineapple on pizza, {}",
            $user,
        );
    }
}
check_valid_pizza!("John", "salami");
check_valid_pizza!("Dave", "sausage");
check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
```
This is the compiler output:

```
error[E0080]: evaluation of constant value failed
  --> src/lib.rs:178:27
   |
20 | check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
   |                           ^^^^^^^^^^^ the evaluated program panicked at '
assertion failed: `(left != right)`
 left: `"pineapple"`
right: `"pineapple"`
You can't put pineapple on pizza, Bob
', src/lib.rs:20:27
```

-

-
They cannot be used places that take string literals. So `#[doc = "foobar"]`cannot be replaced with`#[doc = concatcp!("foo", "bar") ]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#integer-arguments)Integer arguments

# const_format - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/const_format/0.2.36/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/const_format/

## Expand description

Compile-time string formatting.

This crate provides types and macros for formatting strings at compile-time.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-versions)Rust versions

There are some features that require a variety of Rust versions, the sections below describe the features that are available for each version.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-1710)Rust 1.71.0

These macros are available in Rust 1.71.0:

-
`concatcp``integers`,`bool`,`char`, and`&str`constants into a`&'static str`constant.
-
`formatcp``format``integers`,`bool`,`char`, and`&str`constants, and emits a`&'static str`constant.
-
`str_get``&'static str`constant, returning`None`when the index is out of bounds.
-
`str_index``&'static str`constant.
-
`str_repeat``&'static str`by repeating a`&'static str`constant`times`times.
-
`str_splice``&'static str`constant.
-
`map_ascii_case``&'static str`constant to a different casing style, determined by a`Case`
-
`str_replace``&'static str`constant with another`&'static str`constant.
-
`str_split`

The `"assertcp"` feature enables the [ assertcp](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_eq.html)

`assertcp_eq`[macros. These macros are like the standard library assert macros, but evaluated at compile-time, with the limitation that they can only have primitive types as arguments (just like](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html)

`assertcp_ne`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.concatcp.html)

`concatcp`[).](https://docs.rs/macro.formatcp.html)

`formatcp`[§](https://docs.rs#rust-1830)Rust 1.83.0

By enabling the “fmt” feature, you can use a [ std::fmt](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/index.html)-like API.

This requires Rust 1.83.0, because it uses mutable references in const fn.

All the other features of this crate are implemented on top of the [ const_format::fmt](https://docs.rs/fmt/index.html) API:

-
`concatc``&'static str`constant.
-
`formatc``format``&'static str`constant.
-
`writec``write``WriteMarker`

The `"derive"` feature enables the [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) macro,
and the

`"fmt"` feature.[derives the](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html)

`ConstDebug`[trait, and implements an inherent](https://docs.rs/marker_traits/trait.FormatMarker.html)

`FormatMarker``const_debug_fmt` method for compile-time debug formatting.The `"assertc"` feature enables the [ assertc](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc_eq.html)

`assertc_eq`[macros, and the](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc_ne.html)

`assertc_ne``"fmt"` feature.These macros are like the standard library assert macros, but evaluated at compile-time.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#concatenation-of-primitive-types)Concatenation of primitive types

```
use const_format::concatcp;
const NAME: &str = "Bob";
const FOO: &str = concatcp!(NAME, ", age ", 21u8,"!");
assert_eq!(FOO, "Bob, age 21!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-primitive-types)Formatting primitive types

```
use const_format::formatcp;
const NAME: &str = "John";
const FOO: &str = formatcp!("{NAME}, age {}!", compute_age(NAME));
assert_eq!(FOO, "John, age 24!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-custom-types)Formatting custom types

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro,
and then format the type into a

`&'static str` constant.This example requires the `"derive"` feature
and Rust 1.83.0, because it uses `&mut` in a const context.

```
use const_format::{ConstDebug, formatc};
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Message{
    ip: [Octet; 4],
    value: &'static str,
}
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Octet(u8);
const MSG: Message = Message{
    ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)],
    value: "Hello, World!",
};
const FOO: &str = formatc!("{:?}", MSG);
assert_eq!(
    FOO,
    "Message { ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)], value: \"Hello, World!\" }"
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatted-const-assertions)Formatted const assertions

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ assertcp_ne](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html) macro to
do compile-time inequality assertions with formatted error messages.

This requires the `"assertcp"` feature.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use const_format::assertcp_ne;
macro_rules! check_valid_pizza{
    ($user:expr, $topping:expr) => {
        assertcp_ne!(
            $topping,
            "pineapple",
            "You can't put pineapple on pizza, {}",
            $user,
        );
    }
}
check_valid_pizza!("John", "salami");
check_valid_pizza!("Dave", "sausage");
check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
```
This is the compiler output:

```
error[E0080]: evaluation of constant value failed
  --> src/lib.rs:178:27
   |
20 | check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
   |                           ^^^^^^^^^^^ the evaluated program panicked at '
assertion failed: `(left != right)`
 left: `"pineapple"`
right: `"pineapple"`
You can't put pineapple on pizza, Bob
', src/lib.rs:20:27
```
[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

All of the macros from `const_format` have these limitations:

-
The formatting macros that expand to `&'static str`s can only use constants from concrete types, so while a`Type::<u8>::FOO`argument would be fine,`Type::<T>::FOO`would not be (`T`being a type parameter).
-
Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context, [more details in the Integer arguments section](https://docs.rs#integer-args).
-
They cannot be used places that take string literals. So `#[doc = "foobar"]`cannot be replaced with`#[doc = concatcp!("foo", "bar") ]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#integer-arguments)Integer arguments

Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context. so if you only pass an integer literal it must have a suffix.

Example of what does compile:

```
const N: u32 = 1;
assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(N + 1, 2 + N), "23");
assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(2u32, 2 + 1u8, 3u8 + 1), "234");
```
Example of what does not compile:

[§](https://docs.rs#renaming-crate)Renaming crate

All function-like macros from `const_format` can be used when the crate is renamed.

The [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro has the

`#[cdeb(crate = "foo::bar")]` attribute to
tell it where to find the `const_format` crate.Example of renaming the `const_format` crate in the Cargo.toml file:

```
[dependencies]
cfmt = {version = "0.*", package = "const_format"}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo features

-
`"fmt"`: Enables the`std::fmt``"rust_1_83"`feature, requires Rust 1.83.0 because it uses mutable references in const fn.
 This feature includes the`formatc``writec`
-
`"derive"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, provides the`ConstDebug`
 This implicitly uses the`syn`crate, so clean compiles take a bit longer than without the feature.
-
`"assertc"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, enables the`assertc``assertc_eq``assertc_ne`
 This feature was previously named`"assert"`, but it was renamed to avoid confusion with the`"assertcp"`feature.
-
`"assertcp"`: Enables the`assertcp``assertcp_eq``assertcp_ne`
-
`"rust_1_83"`: Makes macros that evaluate to a value become compatible with[inline const patterns](https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.83.0/unstable-book/language-features/inline-const-pat.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

`const_format` is unconditionally `#![no_std]`, it can be used anywhere Rust can be used.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

`const_format` requires Rust 1.71.0.

Features that require newer versions of Rust, or the nightly compiler, need to be explicitly enabled with cargo features.

- Replaces all the instances of `$pattern`in`$input`(a`&'static str`constant) with`$replace_with`(a`&'static str`constant).

- Replaces a substring in a `&'static str`constant. Returns both the new resulting`&'static str`, and the replaced substring.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_splice_out.html)- splice_ - out
- Alternative version of `str_splice`
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_split.html)- split
- Splits `$string`(a`&'static str`constant) with`$splitter`, returning an array of`&'static str`s.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_split_pat.html)- split_ - pat
- Version of `str_split``&'static [&'static str]`.
- [strwriter_](https://docs.rs/macro.strwriter_as_str.html)- as_ - str - Deprecated - `fmt`
- Converts a `&'static StrWriter`to a`&'static str`, in a`const`/`static`initializer.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_.html)- `fmt`
- For returning early on an error, otherwise evaluating to `()`.
- [unwrap](https://docs.rs/macro.unwrap.html)- `fmt`
- Equivalent to `Result::unwrap`, for use with`const_format::Error`
- [unwrap_](https://docs.rs/macro.unwrap_or_else.html)- or_ - else - `fmt`
- Equivalent to `Result::unwrap_or_else`but allows returning from the enclosing function.
- [writec](https://docs.rs/macro.writec.html)- `fmt`
- Writes some formatted standard library and/or user-defined types into a buffer.

- Compile-time assertion with formatting.

- [assertcp_](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html)- ne - `assertcp`
- Compile-time inequality assertion with formatting.

# const_format - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/const_format/0.2.36/target-redirect/const_format/

## Expand description

Compile-time string formatting.

This crate provides types and macros for formatting strings at compile-time.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-versions)Rust versions

There are some features that require a variety of Rust versions, the sections below describe the features that are available for each version.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-1710)Rust 1.71.0

These macros are available in Rust 1.71.0:

-
`concatcp``integers`,`bool`,`char`, and`&str`constants into a`&'static str`constant.
-
`formatcp``format``integers`,`bool`,`char`, and`&str`constants, and emits a`&'static str`constant.
-
`str_get``&'static str`constant, returning`None`when the index is out of bounds.
-
`str_index``&'static str`constant.
-
`str_repeat``&'static str`by repeating a`&'static str`constant`times`times.
-
`str_splice``&'static str`constant.
-
`map_ascii_case``&'static str`constant to a different casing style, determined by a`Case`
-
`str_replace``&'static str`constant with another`&'static str`constant.
-
`str_split`

The `"assertcp"` feature enables the [ assertcp](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_eq.html)

`assertcp_eq`[macros. These macros are like the standard library assert macros, but evaluated at compile-time, with the limitation that they can only have primitive types as arguments (just like](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html)

`assertcp_ne`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.concatcp.html)

`concatcp`[).](https://docs.rs/macro.formatcp.html)

`formatcp`[§](https://docs.rs#rust-1830)Rust 1.83.0

By enabling the “fmt” feature, you can use a [ std::fmt](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/index.html)-like API.

This requires Rust 1.83.0, because it uses mutable references in const fn.

All the other features of this crate are implemented on top of the [ const_format::fmt](https://docs.rs/fmt/index.html) API:

-
`concatc``&'static str`constant.
-
`formatc``format``&'static str`constant.
-
`writec``write``WriteMarker`

The `"derive"` feature enables the [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) macro,
and the

`"fmt"` feature.[derives the](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html)

`ConstDebug`[trait, and implements an inherent](https://docs.rs/marker_traits/trait.FormatMarker.html)

`FormatMarker``const_debug_fmt` method for compile-time debug formatting.The `"assertc"` feature enables the [ assertc](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc_eq.html)

`assertc_eq`[macros, and the](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc_ne.html)

`assertc_ne``"fmt"` feature.These macros are like the standard library assert macros, but evaluated at compile-time.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#concatenation-of-primitive-types)Concatenation of primitive types

```
use const_format::concatcp;
const NAME: &str = "Bob";
const FOO: &str = concatcp!(NAME, ", age ", 21u8,"!");
assert_eq!(FOO, "Bob, age 21!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-primitive-types)Formatting primitive types

```
use const_format::formatcp;
const NAME: &str = "John";
const FOO: &str = formatcp!("{NAME}, age {}!", compute_age(NAME));
assert_eq!(FOO, "John, age 24!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-custom-types)Formatting custom types

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro,
and then format the type into a

`&'static str` constant.This example requires the `"derive"` feature
and Rust 1.83.0, because it uses `&mut` in a const context.

```
use const_format::{ConstDebug, formatc};
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Message{
    ip: [Octet; 4],
    value: &'static str,
}
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
struct Octet(u8);
const MSG: Message = Message{
    ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)],
    value: "Hello, World!",
};
const FOO: &str = formatc!("{:?}", MSG);
assert_eq!(
    FOO,
    "Message { ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)], value: \"Hello, World!\" }"
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatted-const-assertions)Formatted const assertions

This example demonstrates how you can use the [ assertcp_ne](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html) macro to
do compile-time inequality assertions with formatted error messages.

This requires the `"assertcp"` feature.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use const_format::assertcp_ne;
macro_rules! check_valid_pizza{
    ($user:expr, $topping:expr) => {
        assertcp_ne!(
            $topping,
            "pineapple",
            "You can't put pineapple on pizza, {}",
            $user,
        );
    }
}
check_valid_pizza!("John", "salami");
check_valid_pizza!("Dave", "sausage");
check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
```
This is the compiler output:

```
error[E0080]: evaluation of constant value failed
  --> src/lib.rs:178:27
   |
20 | check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
   |                           ^^^^^^^^^^^ the evaluated program panicked at '
assertion failed: `(left != right)`
 left: `"pineapple"`
right: `"pineapple"`
You can't put pineapple on pizza, Bob
', src/lib.rs:20:27
```
[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

All of the macros from `const_format` have these limitations:

-
The formatting macros that expand to `&'static str`s can only use constants from concrete types, so while a`Type::<u8>::FOO`argument would be fine,`Type::<T>::FOO`would not be (`T`being a type parameter).
-
Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context, [more details in the Integer arguments section](https://docs.rs#integer-args).
-
They cannot be used places that take string literals. So `#[doc = "foobar"]`cannot be replaced with`#[doc = concatcp!("foo", "bar") ]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#integer-arguments)Integer arguments

Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context. so if you only pass an integer literal it must have a suffix.

Example of what does compile:

```
const N: u32 = 1;
assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(N + 1, 2 + N), "23");
assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(2u32, 2 + 1u8, 3u8 + 1), "234");
```
Example of what does not compile:

[§](https://docs.rs#renaming-crate)Renaming crate

All function-like macros from `const_format` can be used when the crate is renamed.

The [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro has the

`#[cdeb(crate = "foo::bar")]` attribute to
tell it where to find the `const_format` crate.Example of renaming the `const_format` crate in the Cargo.toml file:

```
[dependencies]
cfmt = {version = "0.*", package = "const_format"}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo features

-
`"fmt"`: Enables the`std::fmt``"rust_1_83"`feature, requires Rust 1.83.0 because it uses mutable references in const fn.
 This feature includes the`formatc``writec`
-
`"derive"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, provides the`ConstDebug`
 This implicitly uses the`syn`crate, so clean compiles take a bit longer than without the feature.
-
`"assertc"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, enables the`assertc``assertc_eq``assertc_ne`
 This feature was previously named`"assert"`, but it was renamed to avoid confusion with the`"assertcp"`feature.
-
`"assertcp"`: Enables the`assertcp``assertcp_eq``assertcp_ne`
-
`"rust_1_83"`: Makes macros that evaluate to a value become compatible with[inline const patterns](https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.83.0/unstable-book/language-features/inline-const-pat.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

`const_format` is unconditionally `#![no_std]`, it can be used anywhere Rust can be used.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

`const_format` requires Rust 1.71.0.

Features that require newer versions of Rust, or the nightly compiler, need to be explicitly enabled with cargo features.

   |                           ^^^^^^^^^^^ the evaluated program panicked at '
assertion failed: `(left != right)`
 left: `"pineapple"`
right: `"pineapple"`
You can't put pineapple on pizza, Bob
', src/lib.rs:20:27
```
[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

All of the macros from `const_format` have these limitations:

-
The formatting macros that expand to `&'static str`s can only use constants from concrete types, so while a`Type::<u8>::FOO`argument would be fine,`Type::<T>::FOO`would not be (`T`being a type parameter).
-
Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context, [more details in the Integer arguments section](https://docs.rs#integer-args).
-
They cannot be used places that take string literals. So `#[doc = "foobar"]`cannot be replaced with`#[doc = concatcp!("foo", "bar") ]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#integer-arguments)Integer arguments

Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context. so if you only pass an integer literal it must have a suffix.

Example of what does compile:

```
const N: u32 = 1;
assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(N + 1, 2 + N), "23");
assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(2u32, 2 + 1u8, 3u8 + 1), "234");
```
Example of what does not compile:

[§](https://docs.rs#renaming-crate)Renaming crate

All function-like macros from `const_format` can be used when the crate is renamed.

The [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html) derive macro has the

`#[cdeb(crate = "foo::bar")]` attribute to
tell it where to find the `const_format` crate.Example of renaming the `const_format` crate in the Cargo.toml file:

```
[dependencies]
cfmt = {version = "0.*", package = "const_format"}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo features

-
`"fmt"`: Enables the`std::fmt``"rust_1_83"`feature, requires Rust 1.83.0 because it uses mutable references in const fn.
 This feature includes the`formatc``writec`
-
`"derive"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, provides the`ConstDebug`
 This implicitly uses the`syn`crate, so clean compiles take a bit longer than without the feature.
-
`"assertc"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the`"fmt"`feature, enables the`assertc``assertc_eq``assertc_ne`
 This feature was previously named`"assert"`, but it was renamed to avoid confusion with the`"assertcp"`feature.
-
`"assertcp"`: Enables the`assertcp``assertcp_eq``assertcp_ne`
-
`"rust_1_83"`: Makes macros that evaluate to a value become compatible with[inline const patterns](https://doc.rust-lang.org/1.83.0/unstable-book/language-features/inline-const-pat.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

`const_format` is unconditionally `#![no_std]`, it can be used anywhere Rust can be used.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

`const_format` requires Rust 1.71.0.

Features that require newer versions of Rust, or the nightly compiler, need to be explicitly enabled with cargo features.

- Compile-time assertions with formatting.
- [assertc_](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc_eq.html)- eq - `assertc`
- Compile-time equality assertion with formatting.
- [assertc_](https://docs.rs/macro.assertc_ne.html)- ne - `assertc`
- Compile-time inequality assertion with formatting.
- [assertcp](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp.html)- `assertcp`
- Compile-time assertion with formatting.
- [assertcp_](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_eq.html)- eq - `assertcp`
- Compile-time equality assertion with formatting.
- [assertcp_](https://docs.rs/macro.assertcp_ne.html)- ne - `assertcp`
- Compile-time inequality assertion with formatting.
- [call_](https://docs.rs/macro.call_debug_fmt.html)- debug_ - fmt - `fmt`
- For debug formatting of some specific generic std types, and other types.
- [coerce_](https://docs.rs/macro.coerce_to_fmt.html)- to_ - fmt - `fmt`
- Coerces a reference to a type that has a `const_*_fmt`method.
- [concatc](https://docs.rs/macro.concatc.html)- `fmt`
- Concatenates constants of standard library and/or user-defined types into a `&'static str`.
- [concatcp](https://docs.rs/macro.concatcp.html)
- Concatenates constants of primitive types into a `&'static str`.
- [formatc](https://docs.rs/macro.formatc.html)- `fmt`
- Formats constants of standard library and/or user-defined types into a `&'static str`.
- [formatcp](https://docs.rs/macro.formatcp.html)
- Formats constants of primitive types into a `&'static str`
- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_fmt.html)- fmt - `fmt`
- For implementing debug or display formatting “manually”.
- [map_](https://docs.rs/macro.map_ascii_case.html)- ascii_ - case
- Converts the casing style of a `&'static str`constant, ignoring non-ascii unicode characters.
- [str_get](https://docs.rs/macro.str_get.html)
- Indexes a `&'static str`constant, returning`None`when the index is not on a character boundary.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_index.html)- index
- Indexes a `&'static str`constant.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_repeat.html)- repeat
- Creates a `&'static str`by repeating a`&'static str`constant`times`times
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_replace.html)- replace
- Replaces all the instances of `$pattern`in`$input`(a`&'static str`constant) with`$replace_with`(a`&'static str`constant).
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_splice.html)- splice
- Replaces a substring in a `&'static str`constant. Returns both the new resulting`&'static str`, and the replaced substring.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_splice_out.html)- splice_ - out
- Alternative version of `str_splice`
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_split.html)- split
- Splits `$string`(a`&'static str`constant) with`$splitter`, returning an array of`&'static str`s.
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_split_pat.html)- split_ - pat
- Version of `str_split``&'static [&'static str]`.
- [strwriter_](https://docs.rs/macro.strwriter_as_str.html)- as_ - str - Deprecated - `fmt`
- Converts a `&'static StrWriter`to a`&'static str`, in a`const`/`static`initializer.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_.html)- `fmt`
- For returning early on an error, otherwise evaluating to `()`.
- [unwrap](https://docs.rs/macro.unwrap.html)- `fmt`
- Equivalent to `Result::unwrap`, for use with`const_format::Error`
- [unwrap_](https://docs.rs/macro.unwrap_or_else.html)- or_ - else - `fmt`
- Equivalent to `Result::unwrap_or_else`but allows returning from the enclosing function.
- [writec](https://docs.rs/macro.writec.html)- `fmt`
- Writes some formatted standard library and/or user-defined types into a buffer.

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/const_format/0.2.36/src/const_format/lib.rs.html

# const_format/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! Compile-time string formatting.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! This crate provides types and macros for formatting strings at compile-time.
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! # Rust versions
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! There are some features that require a variety of Rust versions,
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! the sections below describe the features that are available for each version.
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! ### Rust 1.71.0
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! These macros are available in Rust 1.71.0:
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! - [`concatcp`]:
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! Concatenates `integers`, `bool`, `char`, and `&str` constants into a `&'static str` constant.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! - [`formatcp`]:
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! [`format`]-like formatting which takes `integers`, `bool`, `char`, and `&str` constants,
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! and emits a `&'static str` constant.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! - [`str_get`]:
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! Indexes a `&'static str` constant, returning `None` when the index is out of bounds.
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! - [`str_index`]:
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! Indexes a `&'static str` constant.
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! - [`str_repeat`]:
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! Creates a `&'static str` by repeating a `&'static str` constant `times` times.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! - [`str_splice`]:
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! Replaces a substring in a `&'static str` constant.
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! - [`map_ascii_case`]:
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! Converts a `&'static str` constant to a different casing style,
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! determined by a [`Case`] argument.
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! - [`str_replace`]:
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! Replaces all the instances of a pattern in a `&'static str` constant with
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! another `&'static str` constant.
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! - [`str_split`]:
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! Splits a string constant
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! The `"assertcp"` feature enables the [`assertcp`], [`assertcp_eq`],
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! and [`assertcp_ne`] macros.
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! These macros are like the standard library assert macros,
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! but evaluated at compile-time,
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! with the limitation that they can only have primitive types as arguments
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! (just like [`concatcp`] and [`formatcp`]).
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! ### Rust 1.83.0
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! By enabling the "fmt" feature, you can use a [`std::fmt`]-like API.
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! This requires Rust 1.83.0, because it uses mutable references in const fn.
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! All the other features of this crate are implemented on top of the [`const_format::fmt`] API:
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! - [`concatc`]:
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! Concatenates many standard library and user defined types into a `&'static str` constant.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! - [`formatc`]:
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! [`format`]-like macro that can format many standard library and user defined types into
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! a `&'static str` constant.
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! - [`writec`]:
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! [`write`]-like macro that can format many standard library and user defined types
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! into a type that implements [`WriteMarker`].
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! The `"derive"` feature enables the [`ConstDebug`] macro,
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! and the `"fmt"` feature.<br>
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! [`ConstDebug`] derives the [`FormatMarker`] trait,
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! and implements an inherent `const_debug_fmt` method for compile-time debug formatting.
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! The `"assertc"` feature enables the [`assertc`], [`assertc_eq`], [`assertc_ne`] macros,
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! and the `"fmt"` feature.<br>
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! These macros are like the standard library assert macros, but evaluated at compile-time.
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! # Examples
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! ### Concatenation of primitive types
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! ```rust
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! use const_format::concatcp;
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! const NAME: &str = "Bob";
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! const FOO: &str = concatcp!(NAME, ", age ", 21u8,"!");
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! assert_eq!(FOO, "Bob, age 21!");
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! ```
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! ### Formatting primitive types
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//!
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! ```rust
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! use const_format::formatcp;
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! const NAME: &str = "John";
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! const FOO: &str = formatcp!("{NAME}, age {}!", compute_age(NAME));
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! assert_eq!(FOO, "John, age 24!");
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//!
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! # const fn compute_age(s: &str) -> usize { s.len() * 6 }
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//!
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! ```
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! ### Formatting custom types
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! This example demonstrates how you can use the [`ConstDebug`] derive macro,
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! and then format the type into a `&'static str` constant.
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! This example requires the `"derive"` feature
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! and Rust 1.83.0, because it uses `&mut` in a const context.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!
[115](https://docs.rs#115)#![cfg_attr(feature = "derive", doc = "```rust")]
[116](https://docs.rs#116)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "derive"), doc = "```ignore")]
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! use const_format::{ConstDebug, formatc};
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! #[derive(ConstDebug)]
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! struct Message{
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!     ip: [Octet; 4],
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!     value: &'static str,
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! }
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! #[derive(ConstDebug)]
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! struct Octet(u8);
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! const MSG: Message = Message{
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!     ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)],
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!     value: "Hello, World!",
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! };
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! const FOO: &str = formatc!("{:?}", MSG);
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! assert_eq!(
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!     FOO,
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//!     "Message { ip: [Octet(127), Octet(0), Octet(0), Octet(1)], value: \"Hello, World!\" }"
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! );
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! ```
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! ### Formatted const assertions
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! This example demonstrates how you can use the [`assertcp_ne`] macro to
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! do compile-time inequality assertions with formatted error messages.
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! This requires the `"assertcp"` feature.
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!
[150](https://docs.rs#150)#![cfg_attr(feature = "assertcp", doc = "```compile_fail")]
[151](https://docs.rs#151)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "assertcp"), doc = "```ignore")]
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! use const_format::assertcp_ne;
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//!
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! macro_rules! check_valid_pizza{
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!     ($user:expr, $topping:expr) => {
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!         assertcp_ne!(
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//!             $topping,
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!             "pineapple",
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!             "You can't put pineapple on pizza, {}",
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!             $user,
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!         );
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!     }
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! }
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//!
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! check_valid_pizza!("John", "salami");
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! check_valid_pizza!("Dave", "sausage");
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! # fn main(){}
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! ```
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//!
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! This is the compiler output:
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//!
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! ```text
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! error[E0080]: evaluation of constant value failed
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//!   --> src/lib.rs:178:27
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//!    |
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! 20 | check_valid_pizza!("Bob", "pineapple");
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!    |                           ^^^^^^^^^^^ the evaluated program panicked at '
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! assertion failed: `(left != right)`
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//!  left: `"pineapple"`
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! right: `"pineapple"`
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! You can't put pineapple on pizza, Bob
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! ', src/lib.rs:20:27
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//!
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! ```
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! <div id="macro-limitations"></div>
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! # Limitations
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! All of the macros from `const_format` have these limitations:
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//!
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! - The formatting macros that expand to
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! `&'static str`s can only use constants from concrete types,
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! so while a `Type::<u8>::FOO` argument would be fine,
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! `Type::<T>::FOO` would not be (`T` being a type parameter).
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//!
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! - Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context,
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! [more details in the Integer arguments section](#integer-args).
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! - They cannot be used places that take string literals.
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! So `#[doc = "foobar"]` cannot be replaced with `#[doc = concatcp!("foo", "bar") ]`.
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//!
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! <span id="integer-args"></span>
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//!
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! ### Integer arguments
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//!
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//! Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context.
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! so if you only pass an integer literal it must have a suffix.
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//!
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! Example of what does compile:
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! ```rust
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! const N: u32 = 1;
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(N + 1, 2 + N), "23");
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//!
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(2u32, 2 + 1u8, 3u8 + 1), "234");
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! ```
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//!
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! Example of what does not compile:
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! ```compile_fail
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! assert_eq!(const_format::concatcp!(1 + 1, 2 + 1), "23");
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! ```
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//!
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//! # Renaming crate
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//!
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! All function-like macros from `const_format` can be used when the crate is renamed.
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//!
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! The [`ConstDebug`] derive macro has the `#[cdeb(crate = "foo::bar")]` attribute to
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! tell it where to find the `const_format` crate.
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//!
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//! Example of renaming the `const_format` crate in the Cargo.toml file:
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//! ```toml
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//! [dependencies]
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! cfmt = {version = "0.*", package = "const_format"}
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! ```
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//!
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//! # Cargo features
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//!
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! - `"fmt"`: Enables the [`std::fmt`]-like API and `"rust_1_83"` feature,
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//! requires Rust 1.83.0 because it uses mutable references in const fn.<br>
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//! This feature includes the [`formatc`]/[`writec`] formatting macros.
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//!
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! - `"derive"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the `"fmt"` feature,
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//! provides the [`ConstDebug`] derive macro to format user-defined types at compile-time.<br>
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! This implicitly uses the `syn` crate, so clean compiles take a bit longer than without the feature.
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//!
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! - `"assertc"`: requires Rust 1.83.0, implies the `"fmt"` feature,
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! enables the [`assertc`], [`assertc_eq`], and [`assertc_ne`] assertion macros.<br>
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//! This feature was previously named `"assert"`,
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//! but it was renamed to avoid confusion with the `"assertcp"` feature.
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//!
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//! - `"assertcp"`:
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//! Enables the [`assertcp`], [`assertcp_eq`], and [`assertcp_ne`] assertion macros.
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//!
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//! - `"rust_1_83"`:
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! Makes macros that evaluate to a value become compatible with [inline const patterns].
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//!
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! # No-std support
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//!
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//! `const_format` is unconditionally `#![no_std]`, it can be used anywhere Rust can be used.
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//!
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//! # Minimum Supported Rust Version
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//!
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//! `const_format` requires Rust 1.71.0.
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//!
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//! Features that require newer versions of Rust, or the nightly compiler,
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//! need to be explicitly enabled with cargo features.

# concatcp in const_format - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/const_format/0.2.36/const_format/macro.concatcp.html

```
macro_rules! concatcp {
    () => { ... };
    ($($arg: expr),* $(,)?) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Concatenates constants of primitive types into a `&'static str`.

Each argument is stringified after evaluating it, so `concatcp!(1u8 + 3) == "4"`

`concatcp` stands for “concatenate constants (of) primitives”

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

This macro can only take constants of these types as inputs:

-
`&str`
-
`i*`/`u*`(all the primitive integer types).
-
`char`
-
`bool`

This macro also shares
[the limitations described in here](https://docs.rs/index.html#macro-limitations)
as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#literal-arguments)Literal arguments

```
use const_format::concatcp;
const MSG: &str = concatcp!(2u8, "+", 2u8, '=', 2u8 + 2);
assert_eq!(MSG, "2+2=4");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#const-arguments)`const` arguments

```
use const_format::concatcp;
const PASSWORD: &str = "password";
const fn times() -> u64 { 10 }
const MSG: &str =
    concatcp!("The password is \"", PASSWORD, "\", you can only guess ", times(), " times.");
assert_eq!(MSG, r#"The password is "password", you can only guess 10 times."#);
```

---

# str_index in const_format - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/const_format/0.2.36/const_format/macro.str_index.html

```
macro_rules! str_index {
    ($string:expr, $index:expr $(,)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Indexes a `&'static str` constant.

[§](https://docs.rs#signature)Signature

This macro acts like a function of this signature:

`fn str_index(input: &'static str, range: impl SomeIndex) -> &'static str`and is evaluated at compile-time.

This accepts
[the same  range arguments as str_splice](https://docs.rs/macro.str_splice.html#range-argument)

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use const_format::str_index;
use std::ops::RangeFrom;
assert_eq!(str_index!("foo bar baz", ..7), "foo bar");
assert_eq!(str_index!("foo bar baz", 4..7), "bar");
assert_eq!(str_index!("foo bar baz", 4..), "bar baz");
{
    const IN: &str = "hello world";
    const INDEX: RangeFrom<usize> = 6..;
    // You can pass `const`ants to this macro, not just literals
    const OUT_0: &str = str_index!(IN, INDEX);
    assert_eq!(OUT_0, "world");
}
{
    const OUT: &str = str_index!("hello world", 4);
    assert_eq!(OUT, "o");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#invalid-index)Invalid index

Invalid indices cause compilation errors.

---

# str_repeat in const_format - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/const_format/0.2.36/const_format/macro.str_repeat.html

```
macro_rules! str_repeat {
    ($string:expr, $times:expr  $(,)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Creates a `&'static str` by repeating a `&'static str` constant `times` times

This is evaluated at compile-time.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use const_format::str_repeat;
{
    const OUT: &str = str_repeat!("hi ", 4);
    assert_eq!(OUT, "hi hi hi hi ")
}
{
    const IN: &str = "bye ";
    const REPEAT: usize = 5;
    const OUT: &str = str_repeat!(IN, REPEAT);
    assert_eq!(OUT, "bye bye bye bye bye ")
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#failing)Failing

If this macro would produce too large a string, it causes a compile-time error.

# map_ascii_case in const_format - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/const_format/0.2.36/const_format/macro.map_ascii_case.html

```
macro_rules! map_ascii_case {
    ($case:expr, $str:expr) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Converts the casing style of a `&'static str` constant,
ignoring non-ascii unicode characters.

This nacro is equivalent to a function with this signature:

`const fn map_ascii_case(case: const_format::Case, input: &'static str) -> &'static str`The [ Case](https://docs.rs/enum.Case.html) parameter determines the casing style of the returned string.

[§](https://docs.rs#ascii)Ascii

This only transforms ascii characters because broader unicode case conversion,
while possible, is much harder to implement purely with `const fn`s.

Non-ascii characters are treated as though they’re alphabetic ascii characters.

[§](https://docs.rs#ignored-characters)Ignored characters

These casing styles treat non-alphanumeric ascii characters as spaces, removing them from the returned string:

- `Case::Pascal`
- `Case::Camel`
- `Case::Snake`
- `Case::UpperSnake`
- `Case::Kebab`
- `Case::UpperKebab`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use const_format::{Case, map_ascii_case};
{
    const LOW: &str = map_ascii_case!(Case::Lower, "hello WORLD");
    assert_eq!(LOW, "hello world");
}
{
    const IN: &str = "hello WORLD каждому";
    const OUT: &str = map_ascii_case!(Case::Upper, IN);
    // non-ascii characters are ignored by map_ascii_case.
    assert_eq!(OUT, "HELLO WORLD каждому");
}
const IN2: &str = "hello fooкаждому100Bar#qux";
{
    const OUT: &str = map_ascii_case!(Case::Pascal, IN2);
    assert_eq!(OUT, "HelloFooкаждому100BarQux");
}
{
    const OUT: &str = map_ascii_case!(Case::Camel, IN2);
    assert_eq!(OUT, "helloFooкаждому100BarQux");
}
{
    const OUT: &str = map_ascii_case!(Case::Snake, IN2);
    assert_eq!(OUT, "hello_fooкаждому_100_bar_qux");
}
{
    const OUT: &str = map_ascii_case!(Case::UpperSnake, IN2);
    assert_eq!(OUT, "HELLO_FOOкаждому_100_BAR_QUX");
}
{
    const OUT: &str = map_ascii_case!(Case::Kebab, IN2);
    assert_eq!(OUT, "hello-fooкаждому-100-bar-qux");
}
{
    const OUT: &str = map_ascii_case!(Case::UpperKebab, IN2);
    assert_eq!(OUT, "HELLO-FOOкаждому-100-BAR-QUX");
}
```

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.UpperKebab)

### UpperKebab

Kebab case, eg: `FOO-BAR-BAZ`. Also turns the string uppercase.

# str_replace in const_format - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/const_format/0.2.36/const_format/macro.str_replace.html

```
macro_rules! str_replace {
    ($input:expr, $pattern:expr, $replace_with:expr $(,)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Replaces all the instances of `$pattern` in `$input`
(a `&'static str` constant) with `$replace_with` (a `&'static str` constant).

[§](https://docs.rs#signature)Signature

This macro acts like a function of this signature:

```
fn str_replace(
    input: &'static str,
    pattern: impl Pattern,
    replace_with: &'static str,
) -> &'static str
```
and is evaluated at compile-time.

Where `pattern` can be any of these types:

-
`&'static str`
-
`char`
-
`u8`: required to be ascii (`0`up to`127`inclusive).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use const_format::str_replace;
// Passing a string pattern
assert_eq!(
    str_replace!("The incredible shrinking man.", "i", "eee"),
    "The eeencredeeeble shreeenkeeeng man.",
);
// Passing a char pattern
assert_eq!(
    str_replace!("The incredible shrinking man.", ' ', "---"),
    "The---incredible---shrinking---man.",
);
// Passing an ascii u8 pattern.
assert_eq!(
    str_replace!("The incredible shrinking man.", b'i', "eee"),
    "The eeencredeeeble shreeenkeeeng man.",
);
// Removing all instances of the pattern
assert_eq!(
    str_replace!("remove haire", "re", ""),
    "move hai",
);
// This shows that all the arguments can be `const`s, they don't have to be literals.
{
    const IN: &str = "Foo Boo Patoo";
    const REPLACING: &str = "oo";
    const REPLACE_WITH: &str = "uh";
    assert_eq!(str_replace!(IN, REPLACING, REPLACE_WITH), "Fuh Buh Patuh");
}
```

# assertcp in const_format - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/const_format/0.2.36/const_format/macro.assertcp.html

```
macro_rules! assertcp {
    ($($parameters:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
**crate feature**only.

`assertcp`## Expand description

Compile-time assertion with formatting.

This macro requires the `"assertcp"` feature to be exported.

[§](https://docs.rs#syntax)Syntax

This macro uses the same syntax
for the format string and formatting arguments as the
[ formatcp](https://docs.rs/macro.formatcp.html) macro.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

This macro can only take constants of these types as arguments:

-
`&str`
-
`i*`/`u*`(all the primitive integer types).
-
`char`
-
`bool`

This macro also has these limitations:

-
It can only use constants that involve concrete types, so while a `Type::<u8>::FOO`in an argument would be fine,`Type::<T>::FOO`would not be (`T`being a type parameter).
-
Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context, [as described in the integer arguments section in the root module](https://docs.rs/index.html#integer-args).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#passing-assertion)Passing assertion

```
use const_format::assertcp;
use std::mem::align_of;
assertcp!(
    align_of::<&str>() == align_of::<usize>(),
    "The alignment of `&str`({} bytes) and `usize`({} bytes) isn't the same?!?!",
    align_of::<&str>(),
    align_of::<usize>(),
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#failing-assertion)Failing assertion

This example demonstrates a failing assertion, and how the compiler error looks like as of 2023-10-14.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```

```

# const_format::fmt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/const_format/0.2.36/const_format/fmt/index.html

**crate feature**only.

`fmt`## Expand description

[ std::fmt](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/)-like
api that can be used at compile-time.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

This module requires the “fmt” feature to be exported, and Rust 1.83.0,
because it uses `&mut` in `const fn`s.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-the-formatting-methods)Implementing the formatting methods

Users of this library can implement debug and display formatting by
defining `const_debug_fmt` and `const_display_fmt` inherent methods
with the

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// use const_format::{Formatter, Error};
const fn const_debug_fmt(&self, &mut Formatter<'_>) -> Result<(), Error>
const fn const_display_fmt(&self, &mut Formatter<'_>) -> Result<(), Error>
```
signatures,
and implementing the [ FormatMarker](https://docs.rs/marker_traits/trait.FormatMarker.html) trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-impls)Generic impls

Because the formatting of custom types is implemented with duck typing, it’s not possible to format generic types, instead you must do either of these:

-
Provide all the implementations ahead of time, what `impl_fmt`
-
Provide a macro that formats the type. The `call_debug_fmt`macro is a version of this that formats generic std types.

[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-syntax)Formatting Syntax

The formatting macros all share the formatting syntax, modeled after the syntax of the formatting macros of the standard library.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments)Arguments

Arguments in the format string can be named and positional in these ways:

-
Implicitly positional(eg: `formatc!("{}", 20u8)`):
 Starts at the 0th positional argument and increments with every use.
-
Explicit positional(eg: `formatc!("{0}", 10u8)`).
-
Named, passed to the macro as named arguments (eg: `formatc!("{foo}", foo = 10u8)`).
-
Named, from constant (eg: `formatc!("{FOO}")`): Uses the`FOO`constant from the enclosing scope.
-
Named, from locals (eg: `writec!(writable, "{foo}")`): Uses the`foo`local variable from the enclosing scope, only usable with the`writec`

[§](https://docs.rs#formatters)Formatters

The format arguments can be formatted in these ways:

-
Debug formatting (eg: `formatc!("{:?}", 0u8)`):
 Similar to how Debug formatting in the standard library works, except that it does not escape unicode characters.
-
Display formatting (eg: `formatc!("{}", 0u8)`,`formatc!("{:}", 0u8)`)
-
Lowercase hexadecimal formatting (eg: `formatc!("{:x}", 0u8)`):
 Writes numbers in lowercase hexadecimal. This can be combined with debug formatting with the`"{:x?}"`formatter.
-
Uppercase hexadecimal formatting (eg: `formatc!("{:X}", 0u8)`):
 Writes numbers in uppercase hexadecimal. This can be combined with debug formatting with the`"{:X?}"`formatter.
-
Binary formatting (eg: `formatc!("{:b}", 0u8)`):
 This can be combined with debug formatting with the`"{:b?}"`formatter.

[§](https://docs.rs#alternate-flag)Alternate flag

The alternate flag allows types to format themselves in an alternate way,
written as “#” in a format string argument. eg:`"{:#}", "{:#?}"`.

This is the built-in behavior for the alternate flag:

-
The Debug formater (eg: `formatc!("{:#?}", FOO)`): pretty print structs and enums.
-
The hexadecimal formater (eg: `formatc!("{:#x}", FOO)`): prefixes numbers with`0x`.
-
The binary formater (eg: `formatc!("{:#b}", FOO)`): prefixes numbers with`0b`.

[§](https://docs.rs#additional-specifiers)Additional specifiers

`const_format` macros don’t support width, fill, alignment, sign,
or precision specifiers.

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-formatting)Custom formatting

Arguments can access a [ Formatter](https://docs.rs/struct.Formatter.html) for custom formatting with an

`|identifier|` before the expression.The expression will be evaluated every time it is used in the formatting string.

The expression can evaluate to either a `()` or a `Result<(), const_format::Error>`.

Note: this doesn’t distinguish between debug and display formatting.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#derive)Derive

This example demonstrates how you can derive [ ConstDebug](https://docs.rs/derive.ConstDebug.html), and use it with the

`fmt` API.It uses the “derive” feature

```
use const_format::{Error, Formatter, FormattingFlags, PWrapper, StrWriter};
use const_format::{ConstDebug, try_, unwrap, writec};
use std::ops::Range;
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
pub struct Foo {
    range: Option<Range<usize>>,
    point: Point,
}
#[derive(ConstDebug)]
pub struct Point {
    x: u32,
    y: u32,
}
const CAP: usize = 90;
const fn build_string() -> StrWriter<[u8; CAP]> {
    let mut writer = StrWriter::new([0; CAP]);
    let foo = Foo {
        range: Some(0..10),
        point: Point{ x: 13, y: 21 },
    };
    unwrap!(writec!(writer, "{:X?}", foo));
    writer
}
const STRING: &str = {
    const STR: &StrWriter = &build_string();
    STR.as_str()
};
// The formatter
assert_eq!(
    STRING,
    "Foo { range: Some(0..A), point: Point { x: D, y: 15 } }",
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#no-proc-macros)No proc macros

This example demonstrates how you can use the `fmt` api without using any proc macros.

```
use const_format::{Error, Formatter, FormattingFlags, PWrapper, StrWriter};
use const_format::{call_debug_fmt, coerce_to_fmt, impl_fmt, try_};
use std::cmp::Ordering;
pub struct Foo<T, U> {
    a: u32,
    b: u32,
    c: T,
    d: [Ordering; 3],
    ignored: U,
}
//
impl_fmt!{
    // The type parameters of the impl must be written with trailing commas
    impl[U,] Foo<u32, U>;
    impl[U,] Foo<&str, U>;
    pub const fn const_debug_fmt(&self, f: &mut Formatter<'_>) -> Result<(), Error> {
        let mut f = f.debug_struct("Foo");
        // PWrapper is a wrapper for std types, which defines the formatter methods for them.
        try_!(PWrapper(self.a).const_debug_fmt(f.field("a")));
        try_!(PWrapper(self.b).const_debug_fmt(f.field("b")));
        // The `coerce_to_fmt` macro automatically wraps std types in `PWrapper`
        // and does nothing with non-std types.
        try_!(coerce_to_fmt!(self.c).const_debug_fmt(f.field("c")));
        // This macro allows debug formatting of some generic types which
        // wrap non-std types, including:
        // - arrays   - slices    - Option    - newtype wrappers
        call_debug_fmt!(array, self.d, f.field("d"));
        f.finish()
    }
}
const CAP: usize = 128;
const fn build_string() -> StrWriter<[u8; CAP]> {
    let flags = FormattingFlags::NEW.set_alternate(true);
    let mut writer = StrWriter::new([0; CAP]);
    const_format::unwrap!(
        Foo {
            a: 5,
            b: 8,
            c: 13,
            d: [Ordering::Less, Ordering::Equal, Ordering::Greater],
            ignored: (),
        }.const_debug_fmt(&mut Formatter::from_sw(&mut writer, flags))
    );
    writer
}
const STRING: &str = {
    const S: &StrWriter = &build_string();
    S.as_str()
};
assert_eq!(
    STRING,
    "\
Foo {
    a: 5,
    b: 8,
    c: 13,
    d: [
        Less,
        Equal,
        Greater,
    ],
}\
    ",
);
```

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-formatting-1)Custom formatting

This example demonstrates how you can do [custom formatting](https://docs.rs#custom-formatting-section),
by using a `Formatter` directly.

```
use const_format::{call_debug_fmt, formatc};
// Positional argument
assert_eq!(formatc!("{}", |fmt| fmt.write_ascii_repeated(b'a', 4) ), "aaaa");
// Named argument
assert_eq!(formatc!("{foo}", foo = |fmt| fmt.write_ascii_repeated(b'0', 10) ), "0000000000");
// Repeating a positional argument multiple times
assert_eq!(formatc!("{0}{0}{0}", |fmt| fmt.write_str("hi") ), "hihihi");
// Using debug formatting is no different to display formatting:
assert_eq!(formatc!("{0:?}{0:?}{0:?}", |fmt| fmt.write_str("hi") ), "hihihi");
// But binary/hex formatting, and the alternate flag, do have an effect:
assert_eq!(
    formatc!(
        "{0}\n{0:x}\n{0:X}\n{0:b}\n{0:#x}\n{0:#X}\n{0:#b}",
        |fmt| call_debug_fmt!(array, [3u8, 13], fmt),
    ),
    "\
        [3, 13]\n\
        [3, d]\n\
        [3, D]\n\
        [11, 1101]\n\
        [\n    0x3,\n    0xd,\n]\n\
        [\n    0x3,\n    0xD,\n]\n\
        [\n    0b11,\n    0b1101,\n]\
    ",
);
```

# formatc in const_format - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/const_format/0.2.36/const_format/macro.formatc.html

```
macro_rules! formatc {
    ($format_string:expr $( $(, $expr:expr )+ )? $(,)? ) => { ... };
}
```
**crate feature**only.

`fmt`## Expand description

Formats constants of standard library and/or user-defined types into a `&'static str`.

User-defined types must implement the [ FormatMarker](https://docs.rs/marker_traits/trait.FormatMarker.html) trait
(as described in the docs for that trait) to be usable with this macro.

[§](https://docs.rs#stable-equivalent)Stable equivalent

For an equivalent macro which can be used in stable Rust,
but can only format primitive types,
you can use the [ formatcp](https://docs.rs/macro.formatcp.html) macro.

[§](https://docs.rs#syntax)Syntax

This macro uses the syntax described in
[the const_format::fmt module](https://docs.rs/fmt/index.html#fmtsyntax)

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

This macro has [the limitations described in here](https://docs.rs/index.html#macro-limitations).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use const_format::for_examples::Point3;
use const_format::formatc;
// Formatting a non-std struct.
const POINT: &str = formatc!("{:?}", Point3{x: 8, y: 13, z: 21});
// Formatting a number as decimal, hexadecimal, and binary
const NUMBER: &str = formatc!("{0},{0:x},{0:b}", 10u8);
// Formatting the numbers in an array as decimal, hexadecimal, and binary.
// You can use the name of cnstants from scope, as well as named arguments.
const ARR: &[u32] = &[9, 25];
const ARRAY: &str = formatc!("{ARR:?},{ARR:X},{ARR:b}");
assert_eq!(POINT, "Point3 { x: 8, y: 13, z: 21 }");
assert_eq!(NUMBER, "10,a,1010");
assert_eq!(ARRAY, "[9, 25],[9, 19],[1001, 11001]");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-formatting)Custom formatting.

This example demonstrates how you can access the [ Formatter](https://docs.rs/fmt/struct.Formatter.html) in arguments
to do custom formatting.

For more details on this you can look
[in the fmt module](https://docs.rs/fmt/index.html#custom-formatting-section).

```
use const_format::for_examples::Point3;
use const_format::{formatc, try_};
const P: Point3 = Point3{x: 5, y: 13, z: 21};
const STR: &str = formatc!("{0};{0:#X};{0:#b}", |fmt|{
    try_!(fmt.write_u32_debug(P.x));
    try_!(fmt.write_str(" "));
    try_!(fmt.write_u32_debug(P.y));
    try_!(fmt.write_char('.'));
});
assert_eq!(STR, "5 13.;0x5 0xD.;0b101 0b1101.");
```

# writec in const_format - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/const_format/0.2.36/const_format/macro.writec.html

```
macro_rules! writec {
    ( $writer:expr, $format_string:expr $( $(, $expr:expr )+ )? $(,)? ) => { ... };
}
```
**crate feature**only.

`fmt`## Expand description

Writes some formatted standard library and/or user-defined types into a buffer.

This macro evaluates to a `Result<(), const_format::Error>` which must be handled.

[§](https://docs.rs#syntax)Syntax

The syntax is similar to that of other formatting macros in this crate:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
ẁritec!(
    writer_expression,
    "formatting literal",
    positional_arg_0_expression,
    positional_arg_1_expression,
    named_arg_foo = expression,
    named_arg_bar = expression,
)
```
The syntax is otherwise the same as described in
[the  const_format::fmt module](https://docs.rs/fmt/index.html#fmtsyntax).

[§](https://docs.rs#writers)Writers

The first argument must be a type that implements the [ WriteMarker](https://docs.rs/marker_traits/trait.WriteMarker.html) trait,
and has these inherent methods:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
const fn borrow_mutably(&mut self) -> &mut Self
const fn make_formatter(&mut self, flags: FormattingFlags) -> Formatter<'_>
```
[This example](https://docs.rs#custom-writable-example) below shows how to use this macro
with a custom type.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

Integer arguments must have a type inferrable from context,
[more details in the Integer arguments section](https://docs.rs/index.html#integer-args).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#Ẁriting-a-display-impl)Ẁriting a Display impl.

```
use const_format::{Error, Formatter, StrWriter};
use const_format::{impl_fmt, try_, writec};
pub struct Foo(u32, &'static str);
impl_fmt!{
    impl Foo;
    pub const fn const_display_fmt(&self, f: &mut Formatter<'_>) -> Result<(), Error> {
        try_!(writec!(f, "{},", self.0));
        try_!(writec!(f, "{:?};", self.1));
        Ok(())
    }
}
// Coerces the `&mut StrWriter<[u8; 128]>` to `&mut StrWriter<[u8]>`.
// This is necessary because the `as_str` method is defined for `StrWriter<[u8]>`.
let writer: &mut StrWriter = &mut StrWriter::new([0; 128]);
writec!(writer, "{}", Foo(100, "bar"))?;
assert_eq!(writer.as_str(), r#"100,"bar";"#);
```

[§](https://docs.rs#writing-to-a-custom-type)Writing to a custom type

This example demonstrates how you can use the `ẁritec` macro with a custom type,
in this case it’s a buffer that is cleared every time it’s written.

```
use const_format::marker_traits::{IsNotAStrWriter, WriteMarker};
use const_format::{Formatter, FormattingFlags};
use const_format::writec;
const ARRAY_CAP: usize = 20;
struct Array {
    len: usize,
    arr: [u8; ARRAY_CAP],
}
impl WriteMarker for Array{
    type Kind = IsNotAStrWriter;
    type This = Self;
}
impl Array {
    // Gets the part of the array that has been written to.
    pub const fn as_bytes(&self) -> &[u8] {
        const_format::utils::slice_up_to_len(&self.arr, self.len)
    }
    pub const fn borrow_mutably(&mut self) -> &mut Self {
        self
    }
    pub const fn make_formatter(&mut self, flags: FormattingFlags) -> Formatter<'_> {
        Formatter::from_custom_cleared(&mut self.arr, &mut self.len, flags)
    }
}
let mut buffer = Array{ arr: [0; ARRAY_CAP], len: 0 };
writec!(buffer, "{:?}", [3u8, 5, 8, 13, 21])?;
assert_eq!(buffer.as_bytes(), b"[3, 5, 8, 13, 21]");
writec!(buffer, "{}{}", "Hello, world!", 100u16)?;
assert_eq!(buffer.as_bytes(), b"Hello, world!100");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-formatting)Custom formatting.

This example demonstrates how you can access the [ Formatter](https://docs.rs/fmt/struct.Formatter.html) in arguments
to do custom formatting.

Note that `return` inside arguments returns from the function around the `writec`.

For more details on this you can look
[in the fmt module](https://docs.rs/fmt/index.html#custom-formatting-section).

```
use const_format::for_examples::Point3;
use const_format::{StrWriter, call_debug_fmt, try_, writec};
const P: Point3 = Point3{x: 5, y: 13, z: 21};
let writer: &mut StrWriter = &mut StrWriter::new([0; 128]);
writec!(
    writer,
    "The options are: {}, and {}",
    |fmt| call_debug_fmt!(Option, Some(P), fmt),
    |fmt| call_debug_fmt!(Option, None::<Point3>, fmt),
)?;
assert_eq!(writer.as_str(), "The options are: Some(Point3 { x: 5, y: 13, z: 21 }), and None");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#locals-in-the-format-string)Locals in the format string

This example demonstrates how you can format local variables, by using their identifiers in the format string.

```
use const_format::{Formatter, FormattingFlags, StrWriter, try_, writec};
const fn writeit(mut fmt: Formatter<'_>, foo: u32, bar: &str) -> const_format::Result {
    try_!(writec!(fmt, "{foo},{foo:?},{foo:#x},{foo:#b};"));
    try_!(writec!(fmt, "{bar},{bar:?}"));
    Ok(())
}
let writer: &mut StrWriter = &mut StrWriter::new([0; 128]);
writeit(writer.make_formatter(FormattingFlags::NEW), 100, "hello")?;
assert_eq!(writer.as_str(), r#"100,100,0x64,0b1100100;hello,"hello""#);
```
